The gross revenue (before deduction of charges, including the cost price of Opium) derived from the export of Opium, in the financial years from 1926 to 1929, was as follows:—
(Figures for the calendar years are not available).
The acreage under cultivation in 1929 was 42,186.

section.p: question was addressed to the Prime Minister?

p.membercontribution: : Yes, but it did not say anything about the proceedings in this House.

section.title: OPIUM.
section.p: 4. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Secretary of State for India if he will state what is the amount of opium which has been exported from India during each of the last three years; to what countries the exports have been consigned; what revenue has been derived from these exports; and what is the total acreage now under cultivation for the opium poppy in India?

p.membercontribution: : I am unable to give figures for 1930, but, with the hon. Member's permission, I will circulate a table of the latest available figures.

section.title:
CIVIL AVIATION (TRAINING
SCHOLARSHIPS).
section.p: 5. Major GRAHAM POLE asked the Secretary of State for India whether he will give information, concerning the facilities in the form of scholarships offered by the Government of India during the last year to Indian boys either in this country or in India for training in aeronautics, and the advantage that has been taken of these facilities?

p.membercontribution: : In accordance with the scheme for the training of Indians in civil aviation of which I gave my hon. and gallant Friend particulars on the 5th December, 1929, six students are now under training in this country. The last two of these scholars began their course of training in July last.

section.title:
BRITISH INDIA AND NATIVE STATES
(FINANCIAL RELATIONS).
section.p: 6. Major POLE asked the Secretary of State for India whether the Government of India have now received the report of the committee appointed to prepare a preliminary survey of the financial relations between British India and the Indian States; and whether he will consider the desirability of placing this report upon the Table of the House?

p.membercontribution: : The report referred to by my hon. and gallant Friend is presumably that of the committee appointed last summer by the Government of India to investigate certain facts relevant to the economic and financial relations between British India and the Indian States with a view to these facts being before the Round Table Conference. Copies of the report were distributed to members of the Conference and I am arranging for a copy to be placed in the Library.

section.title: BROADCASTING.
section.p: 7. Major POLE asked the Secretary of State for India whether he will give information concerning the policy of the Government of India in respect of the future organisation and development of the services taken over from the Indian Broadcasting Company; and whether it is proposed to take any steps with a view to reduce the loss incurred on account of these services?

p.membercontribution: : A Central Broadcasting Advisory Committee consisting of re- 780 presentatives of the Legislature and of Commercial interests has been set up and has recommended the adoption of certain measures designed to increase the attractions of broadcasting in India.

section.title:
CONVERSATIONS WITH Mr. GANDHI
(NATIVE PRINCES).
section.p: 8. Brigadier - General CLIFTON BROWN asked the Secretary of State for India whether the Indian Princes and their States have been consulted by the Viceroy and informed by him as to his conversations with Gandhi; and whether their rights or treaties are in any way affected by any arrangements that may be come to?

p.membercontribution: : So far as I am aware the Princes were not consulted during the progress of the conversations. The answer to the second part of the question is No, Sir.
: Is it not possible that some of the rights of the Princes may have been interfered with by arrangements of that sort?
: That is a repetition of the second part of the question to which I have given an answer.

section.p: 12. Captain P. MACDONALD asked the Secretary of State for India what basis of co-operation has now been reached between the Viceroy and Mr. Gandhi; and how it affects the position in relation to the private manufacturers of salt?

p.membercontribution: : The hon. and gallant Member's question was answered by the statement issued on Thursday last.

section.p: 14. Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY asked the Secretary of State for India what is the present position with regard to the boycott on British goods; and whether the economic boycott is continuing?

p.membercontribution: : The Position was explained in some detail in paragraphs six and seven of the Statement which I read to the House on Thursday last.
: Is the night hon. Gentleman aware that there is some ambiguity with regard to the continuance or otherwise of the economic boycott, and could he give any further information on this subject?
: I do not think that it would be wise to attempt to amplify the statement as it was printed and read to the House.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman, in view of the approaching Debate, at least ascertain whether the economic boycott is continuing?
: Of course, the trade figures are constantly under observation and the latest information will be gladly supplied to the House.
: May we take it that the Indians will be allowed to buy where they choose?
: Have Indians not as much right to say "Buy Indian goods" as the British people have to say "Buy British goods"?
: Is there not a very great difference between that and bringing pressure to bear?

section.title: POLICE.
section.p: 9. Brigadier-General BROWN asked the Secretary of State for India if he will state what steps have been taken to show the appreciation of the British and Indian peoples for the work of the police in India, British and Indian, in times of difficulty and danger; and whether the Government of India are taking steps to protect their homes and belongings?

p.membercontribution: : Many well-deserved tributes have been paid by local Governments to the manner in which the Indian police have behaved in circumstances of great difficulty. Special allowances for the police have been sanctioned in several Provinces, as was stated in the House on 23rd February. As regards the second part of the question, I trust danger of the nature suggested no longer exists.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman not aware that, in addition to the local Governments, the Government of India, through Sir James Crerar in the Assembly, have expressed their approval?
: Is it not a fact that credit is equally due to British and Indian police and no reference is made to the British police?
: I think the tributes referred to what we call the police, including British.

section.title: AFRIDIS.
section.p: 10. Brigadier-General BROWN asked the Secretary of State for India what is the present position as regards the Afridis on the Indian frontier; whether they have agreed to terms; and whether the road and defence works are being continued unmolested?

p.membercontribution: : No settlement has yet been reached with the Afridis but there is some reason to believe that the peace party among them is growing in influence. The road and defence works are being continued with very little interference from the Afridis. Since the 1st January detachments of our troops have been actively engaged on only three occasions with small parties of tribesmen.
: In view of the dangerous time in the coming summer, is the Commander-in-Chief satisfied that he has adequate forces to deal with any trouble that does break out?
: Those were the plans which were prepared and considered appropriate, and they are being carried through, I am glad to say, without trouble.

section.title:
INDO-EUROPEAN TELEGRAPH DEPARTMENT
(PERSIAN SECTION).
section.p: 11. Major BEAUMONT THOMAS asked the Secretary of State for India whether his attention has been called to the position of the staff of the Indo-European Telegraph Department in Persia, who have now lost their means of livelihood owing to the handing over of the control of the land lines to the Persian Government; whether any alternative employment has been offered them; and, if not, what compensations have been granted?

p.membercontribution:
: I would refer the hon. and gallant Member to the replies which I gave the hon. and gallant Member for St. Albans (Lieut.-Colonel Fremantle) on the 23rd February, of which I am sending him a copy. I am sending to the hon. and gallant Member a statement containing the main items of the scheme of compensation for officers of the Indo-European Telegraph Department, whose services are being dispensed with. Alternative employment with the Imperial and International Communications Limited
783 has been offered to and accepted by some 74 members of the staff of various grades.

section.title: MOSLEMS AND DEPRESSED CLASSES.
section.p: 18. Major - General Sir ALFRED KNOX asked the Secretary of State for India whether, following the settlement with the Congress party, any attempt is being made to obtain a settlement with the 70,000,000 Moslems and 60,000,000 depressed classes?

p.membercontribution: : By means of the continuing work of the Conference it is hoped to obtain a settlement of the Indian problem which shall be equitable to the minorities.
: Does the right hon. Gentleman not think, after a whole fortnight has been spent in obtaining a settlement, that the leader of the party—
: Does the right hon. Gentleman accept the statement that there are 60,000,000 depressed classes, and is it not a fact that the Simon Report stated that the number was 43,000,000?
: I answered the question I am afraid, without making a detailed effort to check the accuracy of the figures mentioned by my hon. and gallant Friend.

section.title: BRITISH ARMY.
section.p: 19. Sir A. KNOX asked the Secretary of State for India what is the present strength of the British Army in India; and whether all units are up to establishment?

p.membercontribution: : The strength on the 1st January was 61,000 as against a total establishment of 59,770.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman say how that number compares with the number 10 years ago?
: I cannot answer that question without notice.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman answer the last part of the question as to whether all units are up to establishment?
: I cannot give an answer to that without a good deal of research. The aggregate figures are established, but I cannot give without great research a detailed answer to that question.

section.title: INDIAN IMPORT DUTIES (BRITISH GOODS).
section.p: 16. Brigadier - General Sir HENRY CROFT asked the Secretary of State for India whether any representations have been made to the Government of India to the effect that if increased customs duties are necessary preference should be extended to British goods over those of foreign competitors?

p.member: The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY to the BOARD of TRADE (Mr. W. R. Smith)
p.membercontribution: : I have been asked to reply. No representations have been made other than those which I described in my reply to the hon. and learned Member for Moss Side and the hon. and gallant Member for Clitheroe on 4th March. The hon. and gallant Member is no doubt aware that British cotton goods already enjoy in India the advantage of lower customs duties than those applicable to similar foreign goods. This advantage they will continue to enjoy.

: Do I understand that when those proposals were submitted to the Secretary of State no representations were made to see that the increased duties should have preferential effect with regard to Britain?

: I do not think that I can add anything to the reply which I gave the other day when I stated that the whole position was represented to the Indian Government and emphasis laid upon the great anxiety that exists in this country with regard to it.
: Have any efforts been made to see that British goods at least shall receive priority over foreign goods—[Interruption.] It is a very vital question.

section.title: RUSSIA.
section.p: 34. Mr. SMITHERS asked the Secretary to the Overseas Trade Department whether, in view of the fact that British imports from Russia for the last three years total £82,250,000 and British exports to Russia £13,250,000, he will withhold the grant of further facilities under the Export Credits Scheme till this reservoir of credit is used up?

p.membercontribution: : No, Sir.
: Arising out of that very short answer, may I ask why the Government continue to give unnecessary credits to Russia?
: Is it not a fact that this vast balance is being used in order to purchase goods in other countries—in the United States and elsewhere—and what is the advantage to this country?

section.p: 37. Sir WILLIAM DAVISON asked the Secretary to the Overseas Trade Department what special advantages Great Britain has obtained by reason of the trade agreement entered into with Russia by the present Government as compared with the United States of America, who have no trade agreement with Russia; and whether the direct exports from Great Britain to Russia have been greater than the exports from the United States to Russia during the period since the trade agreement has been operative?

p.membercontribution: : With regard to the first part of the question, the Soviet Government have frequently stated that in future their policy will be to deal as far as possible only with those countries with whom some form of Trade Agreement exists? The concrete advantage resulting from the Trade Agreement is an increase in exports of United Kingdom produce and manufactures during the eight months ending 31st December, 1930, as compared with the eight months ending 31st December, 1929. With regard to the second part of the question, exports from the United States were greater than those from the United Kingdom. But during the period of seven months ending 30th November, 1930, as compared with the similar period in 1929, exports from the United States decreased by 6 per cent., whereas exports from the United Kingdom increased by 96 per cent.
: Can the hon. Gentleman give the figures for the exports from the United States and from this country?
: Perhaps the hon. Member will put that question on the Paper.

section.title: BRITISH INDUSTRIES FAIR.
section.p: 38. Mr. DOUGLAS HACKING asked the Secretary to the Overseas Trade Department whether a committee has yet 786 been appointed, in pursuance of the recommendation in the Chelmsford Report, to consider the question of the acquisition of a site and the erection of buildings in which the British Industries Fair may be held in future years?

p.membercontribution: : An unforeseen delay has occurred in settling the constitution and terms of reference for the Committee, but it is hoped that it will be possible to issue invitations to serve on the Committee before long.
: When will it be convenient to the hon. Gentleman for me to put down a further question on this subject?
: Possibly in a week's time I might have some information; I am not certain.

section.title: LEIPZIG FAIR.
section.p: 39. Mr. HACKING asked the Secretary to the Overseas Trade Department how the Leipzig Fair is financed, with special reference to the cost of advertising that fair?

p.membercontribution: : Since my hon. Friend replied to the right hon. Member's question on this subject on the 23rd February, advice has been received from His Majesty's Consul at Leipzig to the effect that the Saxon Diet has now voted £10,000 to the Leipzig Fair, and that the Government of the Reich have not yet definitely refused to grant a subvention. In the circumstances, it appears that the cost of advertising the Spring Fair will be met from the contributions of the Government of Saxony, the Municipality of Leipzig, the Leipzig Chamber of Commerce, and the exhibitors.
: Is this the first time the fair has had assistance from the Government?
: I could not say without notice.

section.p: 40. Mr. HACKING asked the Secretary to the Overseas Trade Department whether any decision has yet been reached in connection with an increased Government grant towards the advertisement of the British Industries Fair?

p.membercontribution: : I regret that it has not been possible to make provision for more than the existing grant of £25,000 in the Estimates for 1931.

section.title: IMPORTED TIMBER (PRICE).
section.p: 70. Mr. THORNE asked the President of the Board of Trade whether there has been any reduction in the selling price of timber imported from Sweden and Finland during the six months ended February, 1931, and the total amount of standards of timber (softwood) imported from those countries for the same period?

p.membercontribution: : I have no information regarding the selling price in this country of timber imported from Sweden and Finland. The average declared import values of soft wood (sawn and planed or dressed) and of pitprops or pitwood imported from these countries in January, 1931, compared with those in August, 1930, show a decline except in the case of pitprops or pitwood from Sweden. The total quantity of soft wood including pitprops or pitwood imported into the United Kingdom and registered during the six months ended the 31st. January, 1931, as consigned from Sweden was 693,000 loads, and from Finland 934,000 loads. Particulars in respect of February, 1931, are not yet available.

: Is my hon. Friend not aware that the price of standard timber both from Finland and Sweden has been reduced on two occasions, due to the fact that the Russians have been imparting timber and have made them reduce their prices?
: Hear, hear. Cheaper houses.

section.title: RUBBER INDUSTRY.
section.p: 71. Sir WILLIAM LANE MITCHELL (for Sir FRANK NELSON), asked the Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies the approximate loss of revenue experienced by the Governments of the Straits Settlements and Ceylon owing to the fall in the price of raw rubber since the removal of the Stevenson restriction scheme?

p.member: The UNDER-SECRETARY of STATE for the COLONIES (Dr. Drummond Shiels)
p.membercontribution: : The revenues of the Colonies named have fallen since 1928, but not more proportionally than that of most other countries. It is quite impossible to say how much is due to the fall in the price of rubber and how much to other causes.

section.p: 75. Sir W. LANE MITCHELL (for Sir F. NELSON) asked the Under-Secre- 788 tary of State for the Colonies if he is aware that, with the price of raw rubber in the neighbourhood of 4d. per pound, the rubber-planting industry in the Straits Settlements and Ceylon is incurring losses; and will he state what His Majesty's Government propose to do to save the industry?

p.membercontribution: : I would refer the hon. Member to the reply given to the hon. Member for Bromley (Mr. Campbell) on the 6th of March.

section.title:
UNITED STATES (BRITISH
IMMIGRANTS).
section.p: 22. Mr. HANNON asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs to what, extent the recent decision of the House of Representatives at Washington that the United States should prohibit foreign immigration for two years will affect emigration from Great Britain and Ireland and from British Dominions and Colonies; and if he proposes to make any representations through diplomatic channels far a modification of those restrictions in favour of the British Empire?

p.member: The UNDER-SECRETARY of STATE for FOREIGN AFFAIRS (Mr. Dalton)
p.membercontribution: : A Bill for the further restriction of immigration to the United States recently passed the House of Representatives, but had not been brought before the Senate when Congress adjourned on the 4th March.

: Have any representations been made through diplomatic channels with a view to safeguarding the interests of Canada and other parts of the British Empire as affected by this decision of the United States?

: I think it would be rather unusual to make representations at this stage, when, as I have already pointed out, the Bill has not been brought before the Senate. I am sure that my right hon. Friend will, naturally, watch the matter from the point of view indicated by the hon. Member.

section.title: CHINA.
section.p: 23. Mr. DAY asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs whether he has any further statement to make on the conditions in China?

p.membercontribution: : There has been no material change in the situation since the reply given to the hon. and gallant Member for the Isle of Wight (Captain P. Macdonald) on the 25th February.

section.title: PETITIONS.
section.p: 24. Mr. BARR asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs if he will give the list of minority petitions received by the secretariat of the League of Nations, during the period 13th June, 1929, to 31st May, 1930, which were declared receivable but whose examination has not yet been finished?

p.membercontribution: : Under the existing rules of procedure, publicity is ordinarily only given to the number of petitions received, the numbers declared to be receivable and non-receivable, and the number of petitions of which the examination by a committee of three members of the Council has been completed. My right hon. Friend regrets that he is not, therefore, in a position to give a list of the petitions to which my hon. Friend refers.

section.p: 30. Mr. BARR asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs if he will explain the grounds on which the committee of three decided that the petition presented to the League of Nations by three Macedonians on 14th January, 1930, could not properly be brought before the Council?

p.membercontribution: : Committees of three members of the Council, when they have completed their examination of a minority petition, make a report to the Council. This report is, however, only circulated to Council members for their information, and is not published unless a special decision to that effect is taken with the consent of the Government concerned. No such decision was taken in this case, and, consequently, my right hon. Friend is not in a position to announce the grounds on which the decision of the Committee of Three was based.

section.title: LIBERIA.
section.p: 31. Earl WINTERTON asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs if the Government of the Republic of Liberia have accepted the recommendations of the recent conference arising out 790 of the report of the committee of the League of Nations to inquire into allegations of slavery in Liberia; and whether the system of forced labour to which exception was taken in the report has now ceased?

p.membercontribution: : The Liberian Government were represented on the committee set up by the Council of the League of Nations, and this committee unanimously adopted the resolutions to which the Noble Lord refers. With regard to the second part of the question, His Majesty's Government have every reason to hope that the expert on general administration, who is now proceeding to Monrovia, will be able to propose suitable action in order to bring to an end the unsatisfactory state of affairs revealed in the report of the Commission of Inquiry.
: Is the effect of the hon. Gentleman's long answer to the second part of the question that this forced labour has not ceased? Has he had any information from His Majesty's representatives there?

: We should not like to commit ourselves to a statement which might turn out to be untrue and damaging to the Liberian Government, who, we believe, are making efforts to improve the position in this respect; but the answer which I gave to the second part of the Noble Lord's question was that we trust that we shall soon get an accurate report of the state of affairs from this gentleman who is proceeding to Monrovia.

section.title:
RUSSIA (DEBTS, CLAIMS, AND
COUNTER-CLAIMS).
section.p:
27 and 28. Mr. SMITHERS asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs (1) how many meetings have been held of the sub-committee dealing with the claims of British holders of Russian bonds; whether this sub-committee has yet submitted any report to the main joint committee on Soviet debts; and whether the Soviet representatives have recognised the validity of these bonds;
(2) whether he will consider the desirability of issuing an annual or quarterly report dealing with the work accomplished to date by the main joint Anglo-Soviet Committee dealing with claims for compensation?

p.membercontribution: : The main Anglo-Soviet Debts and Claims Committee has held 11 meetings; Sub-Committee B (bond-holders' claims) has held two meetings, and Sub-Committee C (miscellaneous private debts, claims and counter-claims) one meeting. These sub-committees have not yet reported to the main committee. The other four sub-committees have not yet met. The conditions of their meeting are at present under discussion between the plenipotentiaries. My right hon. Friend has taken note of the interesting suggestion of the hon. Member for Chislehurst (Mr. Smithers) as to the issue of periodical reports.
: Has any evidence yet been taken from the claimants?
: No, not yet.
: May I ask when the Government propose to bring this farce to a conclusion?
: I doubt whether that is an accurate description of what has taken place, but, if so, the state of affairs when the party opposite was in power was worse, because nothing was done at all.

section.title:
PORTUGUESE WEST AFRICA
(BRITISH SEAMAN'S ARREST).
section.p: 29. Mr. HORE-BELISHA asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs if he is now in a position to make a statement in respect of the representations made by His Majesty's Ambassador at 792 Lisbon to the Portuguese Government in November, 1928, regarding the arrest on the charge of theft of £1 of Mr. A. J. Brewer, who was detained for nine months while awaiting trial in Portuguese West Africa, and subsequently sentenced to 300 days' imprisonment and £18 fine or another 90 days' imprisonment?

p.membercontribution: : My right hon. Friend regrets that the Portuguese Government have as yet been unable to give His Majesty's Government any satisfaction in regard to this long-standing case. He has instructed His Majesty's Ambassador in Lisbon to make further representations to the Portuguese Government.
: Why does the hon. Gentleman allow the Portuguese Government to snap its fingers at us?

section.title: SLAVE TRAFFIC (RED SEA).
section.p: 32. Earl WINTERTON asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs how many instances of slaves being shipped from the African to the Arabian Coasts of the Red Sea were brought to his notice in 1930; and whether, in such cases, any representations were made to the Governments of the country or countries from which the slaves were shipped?

p.membercontribution: : No specific instances of slave trading were brought to my right hon. Friend's notice during the past year, and the second part of the question does not, therefore, arise. It is, I fear, quite possible that shipments of slaves from the African to the Arabian Coast still take place; but the activities of His Majesty's sloops, and the measures taken by the French and Italian Governments, have undoubtedly reduced this traffic to comparatively small proportions.
: I presume that the hon. Gentleman's Department receives periodical reports from the Admiralty as to any cases that may be noticed?
: Oh, yes, we keep in very close touch with the Admiralty.
: Does not this show one of the many uses of the British Navy?
: Yes, Sir; if such a demonstration were necessary, this would afford it.

section.title:
BRITISH AND CONTINENTAL
RESORTS (PUBLICITY).
section.p: 35. Mr. PYBUS asked the Secretary to the Overseas Trade Department whether, in view of the publicity campaign which is being conducted in the advertising columns of the Press and elsewhere in favour of Continental watering places, the method being to belittle English seaside resorts and to emphasise by contrast the absence abroad of restrictions, he will allocate from one of the funds at his disposal a sum of money sufficient to finance a campaign to counteract such propaganda?

p.membercontribution: : Tourists agents and others advertise from time to time the advantages of Continental resorts, but my hon. Friend deplores the method sometimes adopted of belittling British resorts. As regards the suggestion of a campaign in favour of British resorts, I would inform the hon. Member that the Travel Association of Great Britain and Ireland is engaged on a campaign of publicity abroad, in order to increase the number of visitors to this country, which campaign has the support of His Majesty's Government, who make a grant to the Association. If the hon. Member is interested in this question, I would invite him to call at the offices of the Travel Association and examine the work that is being undertaken.
: In view of the very serious importance of this matter, will

section.p: The number of sides of beef graded and marked at Birkenhead was 22,009.
My information is that no beef graded in the Scottish scheme in 1930 was from fat Irish cattle consigned for slaughter at the grading centres.
It is impossible to say what proportion of the beef graded in Scotland or England was from store cattle bred in Ireland and fattened in Great Britain.

42. Mr. PYBUS asked the Minister of Agriculture if he will state the cost of grading the 254,569 sides of Home-killed 794 the Minister earmark a contribution for the express purpose of counteracting this unpatriotic propaganda which urges people to desert English seaside resorts and have the time of their lives abroad—[Interruption.]

section.title: MEAT (GRADING).
section.p: 41. Mr. PYBUS asked the Minister of Agriculture how many sides of Home-killed and Scotch-killed beef were offered for grading in 1930; the number of sides graded at Birkenhead and in Scotland; and what proportion of cattle graded in Scotland were in fact cattle from Ireland?

p.membercontribution: : As the reply is necessarily somewhat detailed, I propose, with the hon. Member's permission, to circulate it in the OFFICIAL REPORT.
: Does the written answer contain any provision for deciding on a fourth grade in which English meat shall be marked "English meat"?
: Will Scotch have to he marked "Scotch-killed meat"?

section.p: The main figures for 1930 are set out in the following table:

and Scotch-killed beef in 1930, showing, separately, wages and expenses of graders; cost of advertising; and salaries or wages and expenses chargeable to members of the permanent staff of the Ministry of Agriculture engaged on work in connection with marking and grading of beef?

p.membercontribution: : As the reply is rather long, I propose with the hon. Member's permission to circulate it in the OFFICIAL REPORT.

section.p: The figure of 254,569 sides of beef quoted in the question represents the number graded and marked in 1930; the total number graded was 272,504. The salaries, wages and expenses of the grading staff and local charges amounted to £10,491; the total cost of advertising and other forms of publicity was £13,350; the estimated amount chargeable to the beef grading scheme in respect of the salaries and travelling expenses of the headquarters staff of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries and the Department of Agriculture for Scotland was about £2,370. The total cost of £26,211 chargeable to public funds was, under all headings, and especially as regards publicity, substantially increased as a result of the difficulties placed in the way of the scheme in the Birmingham area by a section of the meat trade in that city.

section.title: BOVINE TUBERCULOSIS.
section.p: 43. Mr. HURD asked the Minister of Agriculture what progress has been made with the tests in Northern Ireland and elsewhere of the efficacy of serum treatment for bovine tuberculosis?

p.membercontribution: : I am informed that the Minister of Agriculture for Northern Ireland has not yet issued a report on the progress of the work being carried out by the Government of Northern Ireland. Otherwise, I have nothing to add to the reply I gave on the 5th instant to a question put by the hon. Baronet the Member for Caithness and Sutherland (Sir A. Sinclair).
: Is any progress being made in this country?
: If the hon. Member will put down a question about this

section.p: country, I shall be glad to give him the information.

section.title: SUGAR-BEET INDUSTRY.
section.p: 44. Mr. HURD asked the Minister of Agriculture how many sugar-beet producers there were in each of the past two seasons in Wiltshire, Somerset, Hampshire, and Berkshire, respectively; what was their total production; and what steps are in contemplation to enable this production to be continued with profit to the producers?

p.membercontribution: : As the information desired by the hon. Member is somewhat detailed, I will, with his permission, circulate it in the OFFICIAL REPORT.
: Can the right hon. Gentleman answer the last clause of the question, what steps are in contemplation to enable this production to be continued with profit to the producers?
: The answer to that is the recent arrangement that helped the growers to obtain a price, which has been very effective.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman not aware that that shuts out entirely beet growers in very large sections of the country which are remote from factories?
: The arrangement was the best that could be devised for the factories and the growers.

section.p: I am unable to state the number of beet growers in the counties named in 1929 and 1930, The acreage and production of sugar beet were, however, as follow:
In reply to the last part of the question, I would refer the hon. Member to the announcement made by the Prime Minister on the 12th February last, to which I am unable to make any addition.

56. Captain BOURNE (for Captain P. MACDONALD) asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he is yet in a position to state in what districts the Anglo-Dutch group has entered into contracts with sugar-beet growers; and how these contracts affect growers outside the factory areas?

p.membercontribution: : I am not in possession of information to enable me to answer this question.

section.title: FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE (DANISH BACON).
section.p: 53. Mr. HURD asked the Minister of Agriculture if he is aware that the Canadian Government has by order in council put an embargo on Danish bacon on the ground that foot-and-mouth disease is prevalent in Denmark; and if he is considering the means of similarly safeguarding this country from the risks of disease?

p.membercontribution: : I am aware of Press reports intimating that the Canadian Government has issued such an order. I do not propose to take similar action in this country.
: is the right hon. Gentleman basing his policy on recognition of the fact that foot-and-mouth disease exists in Denmark?
: I am basing my answer on what I am led to believe is the right course to take.
: Does the right hon. Gentleman's Department know that foot-and-mouth disease is prevalent in Denmark?
: Yes, my Department is fully aware of that fact.

section.title: IMPORTED POTATOES.
section.p: 54. Mr. DUNCAN MILLAR asked the Minister of Agriculture whether in view of the spread of the Colorado beetle in countries which at present export potatoes to Great Britain, he is prepared to place further restrictions upon the importation of foreign potatoes into this country?

p.membercontribution: : This subject is receiving my close attention but at present I can add nothing to the reply given to my hon. Friend the Member for Ormskirk (Mr. Rosbotham) on 2nd February. I am sending the hon. and learned Member a copy of that reply.

: Is the right hon. Gentleman not aware of these very severe restrictions which are placed in various countries upon British potatoes, and will he not see that similar restrictions are placed in order to prevent diseased potatoes coming into this country?
: Certain potatoes are already excluded. The only question is where the diseases exists, and that is being investigated.

section.title: MARKETING.
section.p: 55. Mr. MILLAR asked the Minister of Agriculture whether it is intended to make use of the services of auctioneers and livestock salesmen and other existing well-organised selling and distributive agencies, under his marketing proposals?

p.membercontribution: : The approval of a scheme submitted by producers under the Marketing Bill is contingent upon the Minister being satisfied that it will conduce to the more efficient production and marketing of the regulated product. I cannot anticipate the lines of any future schemes which only the producers concerned can submit, but I should expect them to involve the minimum dislocation, consonant with efficiency, of the existing distributive channels and trade practices.
: Am Ito understand that the right hon. Gentleman intends to take into account the services of existing agencies, in consultation with the Dominions?
: Of course, we take all matters into account. I hope the hon. Member will not lose sight of the fact that the object of the scheme is to help the producer.
: Is it not also the purpose of the Act to use agencies that are likely to be helpful in securing that end?
: So far as they help the producer, yes, but not otherwise.
: British or foreign producers?

section.title: EMPLOYMENT
section.p: 58. Mr. C. WILLIAMS asked the Minister of Agriculture the total number of male workers on agricultural holdings exceeding one acre on 4th June, 1914, 1925, 1926, and 1927, respectively; and how many of these were adults?

p.membercontribution: : The total numbers of male workers returned as being in employment on agricultural holdings exceeding one acre in England and Wales on 4th June, 1925, 1926, and 1927 were 694,161, 690,343, and 672,185, respectively. The corresponding numbers of adult male workers in these years were 532,814, 535,097, and 519,913. Similar information was not obtained in 1914.
: Can the right hon. Gentleman get any approximate figures for 1914 for the purposes of comparison?
: I will do my best. If I can, I will send them to the hon. Gentleman.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman make them public?
: Certainly, I will do so.

section.title: RIVER OUSE (POLLUTION).
section.p: 52. Mr. HOFFMAN asked the Minister of Agriculture if his attention has been drawn to the wholesale destruction of fish in the River Ouse from pollution; and what steps he proposes to take to deal with the nuisance?

p.membercontribution: : As there is a case at present being heard before the High Court, in which the plaintiff alleges that the proprietors of a certain sugar beet factory are polluting the water of the River Ouse thereby causing damage to the fish therein, and claims an injunction to restrain them from so doing, I cannot properly make any statement at this stage in answer to the question.
: Are the powers that the right hon. Gentleman has to deal with river pollution adequate?
: No, Sir.

section.title:
TRADE DISPUTES AND TRADE
UNIONS (AMENDMENT) BILL.
section.p: 45. Sir KINGSLEY WOOD asked the Prime Minister whether he proposes to introduce any further proposals in relation to the repeal or amendment of the Trade Disputes Act, 1927?
50. Mr. C. WILLIAMS asked the Prime Minister whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce any further measures with a view to amending the Trade Disputes Act, 1927?

p.membercontribution: : Not at present.
: What does the right hon. Gentleman think of the idea of introducing a short Bill repealing the present Trade Disputes Act?
: Does the right hon. Gentleman really admit by his answer that the 1927 Act was a perfect one?
: Sir Kingsley Wood.

section.p: 46. Sir K. WOOD asked the Prime Minister whether he proposes to afford time to the House to discuss the Special Report of Standing Committee C on the Trade Disputes and Trade Unions (Amendment) Bill?

p.membercontribution: : No, Sir.
: Does not the right hon. Gentleman think it would be a good idea—
: Sir Assheton Pownall.

section.title: DUCHY OF LANCASTER.
section.p: 47. Sir ASSHETON POWNALL asked the Prime Minister whether it is intended to appoint a Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster?

p.membercontribution: : A Chancellor of the Duchy is an essential part of the Administration. The office is not at the moment vacant.
: Does that mean that one of the Ministers of the Crown is now holding two offices?

section.title:
NATIONAL EXPENDITURE
(COMMITTEE).
section.p:
49. Mr. HORE-BELISHA asked the Prime Minister if he can state the name
801 of the chairman of the Economy Committee; and when it is expected that they will begin their deliberations?

51. Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY asked the Prime Minister whether the new Economy Committee will inquire into the expenditure of the three Fighting Services; and whether the committee will have the assistance of experts?

p.membercontribution: : I hope before long to make a statement about this committee, but am not yet in a position to do so.
: Has the selection of the Chairman been made or not?
: That part of the answer will be given when the full answer is given.
: That is the question on the Paper. Is it not the right of a private Member to have an answer?
: It is very inconvenient and difficult to give a partial statement. They are working very hard on it. No time is being lost. I propose to make a complete announcement at the earliest date.
: Will the statement contain the information I have asked for?
: The terms of reference will cover that point.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman not aware of the extreme urgency of the question? Is he not able to state approximately when he will be able to reply to a question if placed upon the Paper?
: I cannot. It depends on matters over which I have no control, but which I am trying to bring under control as quickly as possible.

section.title: TELEPHONE SERVICE, BRISTOL.
section.p: 60. Mr. CULVERWELL asked the Postmaster-General whether he is aware that, owing to the rearrangement of underground work in connection with the Bristol automatic scheme, there will be a delay of at least 12 months before resi- 802 dents at Sea Mills can be given any precise information as to when the telephone service can be supplied to them; and whether he will take steps to hasten their connection with the service?

p.membercontribution: : As was stated in the reply to the previous question on the 2nd March, it is hoped that the new cables necessary in the Bristol area, including Sea Mills, will be completed about six weeks' hence, and that service will be made available shortly after for persons on the waiting list. I regret that the information given locally to certain applicants was incorrect.

section.title: IMPERIAL TELEPHONE SERVICE.
section.p: 62. Mr. LESLIE BOYCE asked the Postmaster-General the Dominions with which regular telephonic communication has been established; the average number of calls per week in each case; and whether the number of calls and the revenue therefrom have reached his original expectations?

p.membercontribution: : Radiotelephonic communication is available between this country and Canada and Australia. The average weekly number of calls is about 17 with Canada and about 27 with Australia. The traffic is rather less than was expected. It has doubtless been affected by the trade depression and should increase when general conditions improve.

section.p: 63. Mr. BOYCE asked the Postmaster-General the reasons why regular telephonic communications have not yet been established between the United Kingdom and New Zealand, South Africa and India?

p.membercontribution:
: Experiments are being carried out with a view to extending the Anglo-Australian telephone service to New Zealand by means of switching in Australia; and I hope that it may be possible to open a service between this country and New Zealand in the course of the next few months. As regards South Africa, the Union authorities concerned have declared themselves in favour of the establishment of a Government-owned wireless station near Johannesburg for the operation of a wireless telephone service with this country, but it is understood that they do not feel able to Commit themselves at present to the
803 capital expenditure involved. I understand that the Government of India is in negotiation with the Indian Radiotelegraph Company for the provision of a radiotelephone station for communication with this country, but these negotiations have not yet been completed.

section.title: EAST AFRICAN MAILS (PAYMENTS).
section.p: 64. Mr. BOYCE asked the Postmaster-General what was the total amount paid or payable by the Imperial and local Governments during 1930 to steamship companies for the carriage of mails to and from British territories in East Africa; and whether any, and, if so, how much, of this money was payable to foreign companies?

p.membercontribution: : The necessary inquiries are not yet completed, and I will write to the hon. Member as soon as possible.
: May I ask the hon. Member whether, in addition to looking after East Africa, he is still considering the interests of Lancashire?

section.title: WAGES.
section.p: 59. Mr. WALLACE (for Mr. BOWEN) asked the Postmaster-General if he can give particulars of the pay of full-time established industrial and manipulative classes in the Post Office after the application of the bonus on 1st March, 1931, showing the approximate number of employés in receipt of inclusive remuneration exceeding £2 10s. but not exceeding £3 10s. per week; and the number of part-time employés and their range of pay?

p.membercontribution: : There are approximately 126,000 established full-time industrial and manipulative employés of the Post Office, of whom about 70,000 are in receipt of remuneration, including bonus at the current rate, exceeding £2 10s. but not exceeding £3 10s. per week. The total number of part-time employés is approximately 28,000. Their pay varies according to the number of hours worked and ranges from a few shillings up to about 42s. a week.

section.title: UNDERGROUND AND OVERHEAD WIRES.
section.p: 61. Mr. BROCKWAY (for Mr. SORENSEN) asked the Postmaster-General whether he has considered the resolutions passed by various town councils urging that local amenities should be 804 preserved by Post Office wires being placed underground in urban districts; and what he intends to do in the matter?

p.membercontribution: : I have received a number of resolutions in the sense indicated. Every endeavour is made to interfere as little as possible with amenities when overhead lines are constructed, and underground lines are provided wherever it is possible to justify the outlay. But in a proportion of cases the cost of underground plant would be prohibitive and overhead plant then represents the only method of providing service on an economic basis.
: Has the hon. Member in particular received communications from the councils in Leyton and Walthamstow on this matter, and will he consider the requests that they have made?
: I cannot charge my memory as to whether I have received those particular communications.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman look into the matter?
: Certainly.

section.title:
HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT
(TERRACE PARAPET).
section.p: 65. Mr. KNIGHT asked the First Commissioner of Works for what reason it is proposed to raise the parapet of the Terrace of the Houses of Parliament and to construct a raised platform adjacent to the parapet?

p.member: The FIRST COMMISSIONER of WORKS (Mr. Lansbury)
p.membercontribution: : Following upon the floods of 1928 the London County Council have fixed new standard levels for flood banks. The existing parapet of the Terrace does not comply with the prescribed standard and, in consequence, it has been decided to raise the top of the parapet from 3 feet 6¼ inches to 4 feet 5¾ inches above the Terrace level. As this will affect to some extent the amenity of the Terrace, it has been considered desirable to make a wall walk on the lines of the design at present exhibited in the Tea Room.

: While thanking my right hon. Friend for his reply, may I
805 ask whether this will have the effect of increasing the protection of the smoking room?
: I do not think it will affect the smoking room.
: Can the right hon. Gentleman say whether the London County Council have any jurisdiction over the Royal Palaces?
: They have no jurisdiction, but common sense would dictate that this is the proper course to adopt.

: The right hon. Gentleman, as a student of common sense, will perhaps explain to this authority that this cannot be a precedent, and that Royal Palaces do not come under the jurisdiction of the London County Council.
: I do not think that it is necessary for me to tell the London County Council what I think the London County Council know quite well.
: Was not precedent set by King Canute?

section.title: HOUSING (HUTMENT ESTATES).
section.p: 66. Mr. MILLS asked the First Commissioner of Works the various hutment estates that have been sold by his Department since 1926; whether, in each case, the estates were sold subject to the existing tenancies and the rights and claims of the tenants then in occupation; and whether during the period of ownership of his Department any hutments were claimed for possession under the powers of the Rent Restriction Acts?

p.membercontribution: : I will circulate my reply, which is somewhat long, in the OFFICIAL REPORT.

section.p:
The following estates have been sold since 1926:
Holbrook Lane (Coventry).
Tyler Street, Petre Street and Tinsley (Sheffield).
Dudley.
Scotswood (Newcastle).
Roosegate (Barrow).
and sections of several estates at Woolwich, namely:
Shepherds Farm.
Bostall. 806
Corbett.
Churchfield.
Woolwich No. 3.
East Wickham.
Lodge Lane, and
Tunnel Avenue.
The houses in each case were sold subject to the tenancy agreements and the rights of the tenants. Where necessary actions have been brought in the County Court against tenants in arrear whose tenancies were protected by the Rent Restrictions Acts.

section.title:
ROYAL PARKS (FILM PRODUC
TION).
section.p: 67. Mr. DAY asked the First Commissioner of Works whether he proposes to make any modifications in the present regulations for taking cinematograph views in the royal parks; and will he give particulars?

p.membercontribution: : I must refer my hon. Friend to the answer I gave to him on the 19th May last, a copy of which I am sending him. Since then there has been no change.
: Can my right hon. Friend say whether any modifications have been asked for since that date, and whether they have been refused?
: The hon. Member must put down a question. I cannot carry these things in my memory.

section.title:
ROYAL MAIL STEAM PACKET
COMPANY
section.p: 68. Mr. EDE asked the Attorney-General whether his inquiry into the affairs of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company will include consideration of whether he should recommend that the royal charter shall be withdrawn while the board contains directors responsible for the 1926–1929 accounts?

p.membercontribution: : I regret that I cannot amplify the answer which I gave to my hon. Friend on Monday last, to the effect that in due course every aspect of the matter will come under my review.

: Can an approximate date be given when the House will be in possession of the in-
807 formation which the Attorney-General is getting?
: No, Sir, I cannot give a date at present.

section.title: CROWN PROCEEDINGS COMMITTEE.
section.p: 69. Sir K. WOOD asked the Attorney-General when he proposes to introduce a measure to carry out the recommendations contained in the report of the Crown Proceedings Committee?

p.membercontribution: : In the present state of public business I am not in a position to make any statement on this subject.
: Surely, now that the Attorney-General has got so much more more leisure, he can hurry this up.

section.title: FORESTS (FIRES).
section.p: 72. Major THOMAS asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Board of Trade, as representing the Forestry Commissioners, if he will state what were the causes of the fires which resulted in heavy losses on Government plantations during the year ended 31st March, 1930; and what special steps have been, or are being, taken to prevent such losses in the future?

p.membercontribution: : The causes of the fires on the plantations of the Forestry Commissioners during the year ended 31st March, 1930, were as follow: Railways, 43 per cent. of the total, general public 31 per cent., road engines 7 per cent., from adjoining land 6 per cent., unknown 6 per cent., probably incendiaries 3 per cent., Commission's employés 2 per cent., and miscellaneous 2 per cent. The Commission's methods of forest fire protection and control were reviewed, and revised instructions issued.
: Is this property insured?
: No.

section.title: POOR LAW RELIEF (KENT).
section.p: 73. Mr. MILLS asked the Minister of Health if he is aware that the public 808 assistance committees of Kent are giving to applicants for relief 36 hours' work, for which they have paid 5s. 6d. in cash and 5s. 6d. in kind as total payment; and whether, in view of the distress caused by these decisions, he will consider the question of task-work with a view to recommending approved scales of relief?

p.member: The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY to the MINISTRY of HEALTH (Miss Lawrence)
p.membercontribution: : My right hon. Friend is aware that the Kent County Council have started in several areas arrangements under Article 6 of the Relief Regulation Order, 1930, for setting to work, training and instructing men in receipt of relief, and that the hours of work, inclusive of an hour for dinner, are approximately as stated. Payment of half the relief in kind is in accordance with Article 7 of the Order. The amount of relief provided is that which is judged necessary by the public assistance authority in carrying out their obligation to relieve destitution and must be regarded from that point of view and not as payment of wages for work or as in relation to the work done.

: Is the hon. Lady aware that these people have been engaged in doing work usually done by landscape gardeners and are receiving a scandalous rate of remuneration as an excuse for so-called Poor Law relief? I want particularly to ask the Department what steps they have in mind to counteract this abuse of the ordinary fair wages rates?
: If the hon. Member has any information to give me as to the nature of the work there, I shall be very grateful to receive it?
: Is it not a fact that the regulation does not specify that any specific number of hours shall be worked?
: That is true. The hours are not specified.

: Will the hon. Lady take into consideration the fact that, if an unemployed man, the father of a family, is asked to do 36 hours task-work there is very little opportunity for him to register or to search for employment?

: Is the hon. Lady aware of the very strong feeling in regard to this matter not only in Kent but
809 in London and elsewhere, and cannot she take steps to revise the present arrangement under which this work is carried out?

: I am aware that in some areas exception is taken to the manner in which local authorities are carrying out the work; I am also aware that in certain other areas very successful work is being carried on.
: Is not the rigour of these tasks the result of instructions given by her Department?

: The instructions sent out by the Department say that the work should be suitable for the age and physical capacity and education of those concerned, and my right hon. Friend feels that often where men are suffering from prolonged unemployment, training elsewhere and wise dieting are of benefit to the recipients.

section.title: PALESTINE.
section.p: 76. Mr. SHILLAKER asked the Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies whether his attention has been called to the danger of religious disturbances in Jerusalem at Easter; and what steps it is proposed to take to ensure that there shall be no rioting or breaches of the peace?

p.membercontribution: : No, Sir, my Noble Friend's attention has not been specially drawn to this matter, but the local authorities will take whatever steps may be necessary.
: Is the hon. Member aware that there have been serious disturbances between Christian churches in Jerusalem at Easter, and will he take steps to prevent disturbances this year?
: Yes, I am aware that there is always a danger of these disturbances at Easter, but the Palestine Administration is well aware of it and may be relied upon to take the necessary precautions.

section.title:
ROYAL NAVY (NEW CON-
STRUCTION).
section.p: 77. Mr. HORE-BELISHA asked the First Lord of the Admiralty, with reference to the naval construction programme 810 of 1931, whether he can say in which of the Royal Dockyards the two cruisers, one leader, two stoops, one submarine, and the tender for His Majesty's Ship "Vernon" will be built?

p.member: The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY to the ADMIRALTY (Mr. Ammon)
p.membercontribution: : My right hon. Friend hopes to make a statement on this matter on Wednesday.
: Can the hon. Member say whether the fact that no cruiser has been allotted to Devonport will mean a decrease in employment?
: No, there will be no decrease in employment there.

section.title:
UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT
(JUVENILES).
section.p: 78. Mr. MILLS asked the Minister of Labour if she is aware that girls under the age of 18 years, who are attending evening classes as a condition of receiving the 5s. benefit to unemployed young persons, are being compelled to buy material for hats, frocks and other articles out of that amount; and if she will inquire into the matter with a view to relieving the parents of such young persons of this burden?

p.member: The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY to the MINISTRY of LABOUR (Mr. Lawson)
p.membercontribution: : My right hon. Friend has made inquiry into a case of this kind which my hon. Friend brought to her notice. In that case fee-paying students were required to supply certain materials and owing to a misunderstanding this was applied to girls attending as a condition for the receipt of benefit. This was stopped as soon as attention was drawn to it.

section.title:
ELECTRICITY DISTRIBUTING
COMPANIES.
section.p: 81. Mr. MUGGERIDGE asked the Minister of Transport the names of electricity distributing companies which have capitalised undistributed profits; the aggregate amount of profits capitalised, and the amount so capitalised during the last two years for which accounts are available; and whether such capitalisation of profits during the period has been accompanied by reductions in charges for electricity?

p.member: The MINISTER of TRANSPORT (Mr. Herbert Morrison)
p.membercontribution: : I am circulating in the OFFICIAL REPORT a statement giving

tr.td: THE FOLLOWING STATEMENT in respect of Electricity Supply Companies other than the London Companies* shows the amount capitalised out of undistributed profits which were earned in past years, carried to Reserve and employed in providing capital assets.
Aggregate amount capitalised from commencement of Company.
Banbury and District Electric Supply Co., Ltd.
Bournemouth and Poole Electric Supply Co., Ltd.
Bridgwater and District Electric Supply and Traction Co., Ltd.(a)
Burgess Hill and District Electric Supply Co., Ltd.
Colne Valley Electric Supply Co., Ltd.
Foots Cray Electricity Supply Co., Ltd.
Lewes and District Electric Supply Co., Ltd.
Market Drayton Electric Light and Power Co., Ltd.
Midland Electric Corporation for Power Distribution, Ltd.
Ramsgate and District Electric Supply Co., Ltd.
Weston-super-Mare and District Electric Supply Co., Ltd.
Windermere and District Electricity Supply Co., Ltd.
Wycombe (Borough) Electric Light and Power Co., Ltd.
Scottish Southern Electric Supply Co., Ltd.

* The capitalisation of the free reserves of the London Companies to a prescribed extent was part of the general settlement between the London County Council and the London Companies confirmed by the London Electricity No. 1 and No. 2 Acts of 1925, such settlement containing provision for the fixing of standard prices, for regulating prices and dividends and for securing to consumers a proper share of any subsequent economies.

(c) In the case of the Windsor Company the capitalisation of Reserves was permitted under a Special Order of 1927 which also prescribed a sliding scale of price and dividend.

NOTE.—The above Schedule excludes the sum of £600,000 representing reserves capitalised by Edmundsons Electricity Corporation Ltd. since the operations of this Company cover other matters besides the supply of electricity and the capital attributable to the three authorised electricity undertakings which they operate constitutes only a small proportion of their total capital.
Of the above-mentioned Companies who capitalised reserves during the years 1928 and 1929 contemporary reductions in prices were made by all except those marked (a) in the Table.

section.title: LOTTERIES AND SWEEPSTAKES.
section.p: 80. Sir. W. DAVISON asked the Secretary of State for the Home Department whether in view of the additional evidence
the particulars which my hon. Friend desires.
recently submitted to him that there is a general demand for a clarification of the law relating to lotteries, raffles and sweepstakes, he is now prepared to take steps in the matter?

p.member: The SECRETARY of STATE for the HOME DEPARTMENT (Mr. Clynes)
p.membercontribution: : I have received from the hon. Member certain documents, including a statement signed by a number of hon. Members representing that the law relating to raffles and sweepstakes requires the immediate attention of the Home Office. I have carefully considered this material, but, as I have informed the hon. Member, I am unable to regard it as proof of any general demand of the kind to which I referred in my reply to the hon. Member for Central Southwark (Mr. Day) on the 11th December last, namely, a general demand that I should look into the question of setting up a committee to investigate, as a practical question, the conditions and safeguards which would be necessary and appropriate if lotteries were to be permitted as a method of raising money for approved public purposes. I have received representations from several quarters protesting against the proposal that sweepstakes should be legalised for the purpose of assisting charitable objects.

: Does the right hon. Gentleman not think that the memorial which I submitted to him covers the point which he raised, namely, that the matter should be inquired into, and will he appoint a committee to see what safeguards are required in order that lotteries or sweepstakes for public purposes may be legalised?

: As my reply indicates I did not regard the evidence which the hon. Member was good enough to supply to me as answering the suggestion which I made, that, if a general demand was shown to me, I would consider it. To a very great extent, the evidence submitted by the hon. Member has been balanced by opposite evidence.

: What evidence of a general demand would the right hon. Gentleman accept? Is he aware that I submitted a memorial sent by Saint Batholomew's Hospital signed by 3,000 people, of whom 2,000 were in the affirmative?
: That cannot fairly be described as indicating a general demand.
: Why are the Government so opposed to setting up a committee?
: Many others beside the Government are opposed to setting up a committee.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman say what he means by a general demand?
: I have done so.

section.title: TITHE RENTCHARGE.
section.p: 57. Mr. GRANVILLE asked the Minister of Agriculture if he will consider the introduction of legislation to make tithe payment a national charge?

p.membercontribution: : I cannot hold out any hope of introducing legislation on the lines suggested by the hon. Member.

section.title: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE.

p.membercontribution: : Will the Prime Minister kindly state what is the business for Friday next?

: The Report stage of the Supplementary Estimates for the Mines Department will be taken as the first Order on Friday, 13th March, and will be followed by the business already announced—further stages of the Small Landholders and Agricultural Holdings (Scotland) Bill.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the second Order, the Smallholders Bill, will take the whole day, and more?
: That may be so, but we just have to wait and see. That is the business as announced.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman see that we get a day ensured in future for the Bill?
: I hope it will not be necessary.

section.p: Ordered, "That the Proceedings on Report of Supply [23rd February] be exempted, at this day's Sitting, from the provisions of the Standing Order (Sittings of the House)."—[The Prime Minister.]

section.title: CHAIRMEN'S PANEL.
section.p: Mr. Frederick Hall reported from the Chairmen's Panel; That they had appointed Mr. James Brown to act as Chairman of the Standing Committee on Scottish Bills (in respect of the Probation of Offenders (Scotland) Bill; and Lieut.-Colonel Sir A. Lambert Ward to act as Chairman of Standing Committee C (in respect of the Mining Industry (Welfare Fund) Bill, and the Ancient Monuments Bill [Lords]).
Report to lie upon the Table.

section.title: STANDING COMMITTEE B.
section.p: Mr. Frederick Hall reported from the Committee of Selection; That they had discharged the following Member from Standing Committee B (added in respect of the Agricultural Marketing Bill): Mr. Attlee; and had appointed in substitution: Mr. MacLaren.

section.title: STANDING COMMITTEE C.
section.p: Mr. Frederick Hall further reported from the Committee: That they had discharged the following Member from Standing Committee C (added in respect of the Mining Industry (Welfare Fund) Bill): Major Llewellin; and had appointed in substitution: the Marquess of Clydesdale.
Reports to lie upon the Table.

body.p: Dr. PETERS asked the Attorney-General whether consideration will be given to the question of introducing legislation to fix an age limit for magistrates who shall be allowed to sit and adjudicate, so that magistrates of over the age of 80 years or 75 years, or as may be determined by Statute, may retire from active administration of the law whilst still retaining the title of justice of the peace?

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: The Lord Chancellor does not consider it desirable 816 to introduce legislation as suggested in the question, as it is inexpedient to establish a rigid rule fixing the age at which justices of the peace, who give their services voluntarily, should retire. It is the duty of advisory committees to inform the Lord Chancellor from time to time of those magistrates who are no longer able to fulfil their responsibilities, and when this information reaches the Lord Chancellor such action is taken as is appropriate to the particular case. It must be borne in mind that there are many other duties to be performed by justices in addition to administering justice in court which can suitably be performed by men of advanced age.

Sir N. GRATTAN-DOYLE asked the President of the Board of Trade when negotiations will be opened with the German Government with a view to securing reductions of the German import duties on British goods; and what have been the terms of the preliminary correspondence?

Mr. W. R. SMITH: The present position is that proposals have been sent to the German Government conveying the desires of His Majesty's Government in regard to tariff reductions. As regards the last part of the question, I would refer the hon. Member to the reply given by my hon. Friend the Secretary for the Mines Department to the right hon. Gentleman the Member for West Woolwich (Sir K. Wood) and the hon. and gallant Member for Clitheroe (Sir W. Brass) on 18th February.

Mr. FREEMAN asked the Minister of Labour how many persons have been transferred from the depressed mining areas of Breconshire for each year; the places they have come from; and to what areas they have been drafted?
Miss BONDFIELD: Statistics giving the numbers transferred from particular areas are not available.

Captain P. MACDONALD asked the Minister of Labour how many men have been transferred to the Isle of Wight from the distressed areas during the past 12 months; whether work has been found for them; and, if so, of what kind?

Miss BONDFIELD: The number of men transferred to the Isle of Wight during the 12 months ended 23rd February, 1931, was 132. Transfers are only made where employment is in view for the men concerned, but details of the employment found are not available.
Mr. WHITE asked the Minister of Labour the number of casual labourers

tr.td: Estimated number of insured persons at preceding July.
Separate figures for casual, skilled and semi-skilled workers are not available.

body.p: Dr. PHILLIPS asked the Minister of Labour what schemes submitted by the local authority and by other public bodies, respectively, to relieve unemployment in Sunderland have been agreed to; what schemes, if any, have been refused or are now under consideration; and the amounts of the grants in each case?

Miss BONDFIELD: 39 schemes submitted by the Sunderland Town Council, and four by other public bodies in Sunderland, have been approved. 10 schemes have been refused and eight are under consideration. The estimated cost of the schemes approved is £912,633.
Mr. FREEMAN asked the Home Secretary the number of accidents, fatal and

compared with the number of skilled and semi-skilled persons employed in the building industry in January of each year from 1926 to 1931, and the number and percentage of unemployed persons in the industry at the same dates?

Miss BONDFIELD: Statistics of the numbers of workers employed in the various industries are available only for July in each year. The following table shows the numbers of insured persons classified as belonging to the building industry at July of 1925 to 1930, and the number and percentage recorded as unemployed in Great Britain in January of each year from 1926 to 1931.
otherwise, caused by wild animals in circuses and travelling menageries during each of the last five years?
Mr. CLYNES: I can only refer the hon. Member to the reply which I gave to the hon. Member for Reading (Dr. Hastings) on the 4th instant.

Mr. FREEMAN asked the Home Secretary the number of local authorities who have taken advantage of the Performing Animals (Regulation) Act of 1925 to appoint officers to visit places where performing animals are trained or exhibited?

Mr. CLYNES: I would remind the hon. Member that the Act provides (Section 3 (1)) for inspection either by the police or by any officer of the local authority duly authorised in that behalf. I have no particulars of such authorisa-
819 tions. In many places the inspection is done by the police. In these circumstances, I do not think that any useful purpose would be served by circularising the local authorities for details of authorisations.
Dr. PETERS asked the Home Secretary how many persons are at present undergoing detention in Borstal institutions and in reformatories or industrial schools, respectively?

Mr. CLYNES: On 3rd March, 1,481 persons were undergoing detention in Borstal institutions. On 28th February, there were 2,103 boys and girls in reformatory schools and 3,889 boys and girls in industrial schools who were sent to these schools by order of Court.

Dr. PETERS asked the Home Secretary the number of persons sentenced to detention in Borstal institutions for whom there is no room in such institutions and who are now located in His Majesty's prisons?

Mr. CLYNES: Youths sentenced to Bostal detention are in the first instance brought to the collecting centre at Wormwood Scrubs for the purpose of examination and investigation before it is decided to which of the Borstal institutions each youth shall be allocated. As explained in the answer I gave on the 12th ultimo to a question put by the hon. Member for Sutton (Viscountess Astor), the effect of the pressure on the accommodation at these institutions is that the time spent at Wormwood Scrubs is in many cases longer than would normally be necessary for investigation purposes.
Captain CAZALET asked the Home Secretary what is the official cost per head to the State of the boys in the Borstal institute?
Mr. CLYNES: The net cost to the Prison Vote of a boy in a Borstal institution was, in respect of the year ended 31st March, 1930, £58 18s. 6d.
Mr. NAYLOR asked the Home Secretary the number of persons in the 820 borough of Southwark who were committed to prison for non-payment of rates in the year 1930?
Mr. CLYNES: The figures collected by the Home Office are not recorded or tabulated so as to give the information desired.

Mr. BRACKEN asked the Secretary of State for India whether he can give a list of the places where salt could be collected or made and sold free of tax under certain administrative provisions of the Government of India previous to this year?
Mr. BENN: I regret that I have no information on the point.

Sir N. GRATTAN-DOYLE asked the Secretary of State for India whether he has any information concerning the protest made by French gilders against the new Indian tariff rates; whether any approach in this matter has been made by the French Government to the Government of India; and, if so, what has been the reply?

Mr. BENN: No official representations have been received by His Majesty's Government in the United Kingdom from the French Government protesting against the protective duties imposed by the Indian Gold Thread Industry (Protection) Act, 1931, and so far as I am aware the answer to the second part of the question is in the negative.
Major POLE asked the Secretary of State for India what steps the Government of India contemplate taking with regard to placing their views before the Parliamentary Joint Committee on East Africa?
Mr. BENN: A despatch from the Government of India has already been communicated to the committee, and they propose to depute a representative to give oral evidence.

Mr. D. G. SOMERVILLE asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs the names of the members of the purchasing commission who will under the China Indemnity Bill lay out the money in this country in the purchase of railway materials?

Mr. DALTON: I would refer the hon. Member to the reply given to the hon. Member for Hallam (Mr. Louis Smith) on 2nd February. My right hon. Friend is communicating a list of names of persons willing to serve on the Commission to the Chinese Government, but he must await the latter s decision before it is possible to make any further announcement.

Sir N. GRATTAN-DOYLE asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs whether steps are being taken to secure a preference for British materials for use in connection with any part of the refund to China of the British Boxer indemnity which is to be used for railway reorganisation and reconstruction?

Mr. DALTON: The answer is in the affirmative. I would refer the hon. Member to the terms of the Agreement with the Chinese Government set out in Command Paper 3715, and to Section 2 of the China Indemnity (Application) Act.

Mr. LLEWELLYN-JONES asked the Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs the number of minority petitions which were received by the secretariat of the League of Nations between 13th June, 1929, and 31st May, 1930, and how many of these petitions were declared to be non-receivable; and whether he will circulate the list of such petitions?

Mr. DALTON: The number of minority petitions received by the secretariat of the League of Nations between 13th June, 1929, and 31st May, 1930, was 57, of which 31 were declared to be receivable and 26 non-receivable. Petitions declared to be non-receivable are not circulated to members of the Council, and my right hon. Friend is, therefore, unable to give the information desired in the last part of the question.

Sir K. WOOD asked the First Commissioner of Works whether he has had his attention drawn to complaints of the unsuitability of the old Town Hall, Woolwich, as a Court of Justice; and whether he is taking any action in the matter?

Mr. LANSBURY: The answer to the first part of the question is in the affirmative; in regard to the second part, I am not satisfied that the complaints are such as to justify the provision of alternative accommodation.
Dr. PETERS asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer what was the total sum paid to retired officers of His Majesty's Army, Navy and Air Force, respectively, for the year ended 31st December, 1930?

Mr. PETHICK-LAWRENCE: Excluding cases falling within the administration of the Ministry of Pensions, the-sums were approximately as follow:
£
Naval and marine officers … 2,559,000
Army officers … 3,413,000
Royal Air Force officers … 87,000

Mr. LLEWELLYN-JONES asked the Minister of Transport when he proposes to lay the Highway Code before both Houses of Parliament, with a view to its being approved in accordance with the provisions of Section 45 of the Road Traffic Act, 1930?
Mr. HERBERT MORRISON: The preparation of the Highway Code is now complete, and I hope to lay it before Parliament very shortly.

Sir K. WOOD asked the Minister of Transport whether his attention has been called to a recent accident at Camomile Bottom, Blackheath, and the observations of the Metropolitan magistrate in a case arising therefrom, and particularly the suggestion that the island should be
823 again inspected to see whether any further public safeguards can be devised; and whether he is taking any action in the matter?

Mr. HERBERT MORRISON: I am aware of the suggestions made for the improvement of the lighting at Camomile Bottom, Blackheath, and arrangements have recently been made for the provision of reflector signs and of additional illuminated signs in each of the converging roads. The locality is being kept under observations, and if further illumination is considered necessary the position will be reviewed.

section.title:
ELECTRICITY CHARGES, CHAT-
HAM AND GILLINGHAM.

body.p: (2) whether he will take steps to see that the inhabitants of the Dorland estate, in the borough of Chatham, who are supplied with electricity from Gillingham mains may be charged at the Gillingham electricity rates instead of the Rochester rates?

Mr. HERBERT MORRISON: With regard to the first question, I understand that negotiations are at present taking place between the Kent Electric Power Company and the borough councils of Chatham and Rochester with regard to the supply of electricity in those boroughs, including an offer by the company to charge the same rates as operate in Gillingham. These negotiations are not yet concluded. With regard to the second question, the supply to the Dorland Estate will be given by the company at the same rates as prevail in Gillingham. Any supply at present being given to this estate from the Gillingham mains is in the nature of a temporary arrangement between the company and the corporation.

section.title: INTERNATIONAL ARBITRATION.

p.member: The SECRETARY of STATE for FOREIGN AFFAIRS (Mr. Arthur Henderson)
p.membercontribution:
: I beg to move, "That this House approves of accession, in respect of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and all parts of the British Empire which are not separate Members of the League of Nations, to Chapters I, II, III, and IV of the General Act for the Pacific Settlement of International Disputes, subject to the conditions set forth in Annex 2 to Command Paper No. 3803." In submitting this Motion I would at the outset remind the House that a year ago, on 27th January, 1930, it gave its approval to the signing and ratification of the Optional Clause.
