Macdonald, Capt. P. D. (I. of W.)
Monsell, Eyres, Com. Rt. Hon. Sir B.
Newman, Sir R. H. S. D. L. (Exeter)

section.p: Original Question put, and agreed to.

section.title:
WAGES &C., OF OFFICERS AND MEN OF THE
ROYAL NAVY AND ROYAL MARINES, AND
CIVILIANS EMPLOYED ON FLEET SERVICES.
section.p: Resolved, "That a sum, not exceeding £13,686,000, be granted to His Majesty, to defray the Expense of Wages, etc., of Officers and Men of the Royal Navy and Royal Marines, and Civilians employed on the Fleet Services, which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st day of March, 1932."

section.title:
WORKS, BUILDINGS, AND REPAIRS, AT
HOME AND ABROAD.
section.p: Resolved, "That a sum, not exceeding £2,288,500, be granted to His Majesty, to defray the Expense of Works, Buildings, and Repairs, at Home and abroad, including the cost of Superintendence, Purchase of Sites, Grants, and other Charges connected therewith, which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st day of March, 1932."

section.title: VICTUALLING AND CLOTHING FOR THE NAVY.
section.p:
Resolved, "That a sum, not exceeding £3,401,200, be granted to His Majesty, to defray the
1353 Expense of Victualling and Clothing for the Navy, including the cost of Victualling Establishments at Home and abroad which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st day of March, 1932."

section.title: NAVY SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATE, 1930.
section.p: Resolved, "That a Supplementary sum, not exceeding £495,000, be granted to His Majesty, to defray the Charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending on the 31st day of March,, 1931, for Expenditure beyond the sum already provided in the grants for Navy Services for the year."

section.title: NAVY (EXCESS), 1929.
section.p: Resolved, "That a sum, not exceeding £122,770 1s. 11d., be granted to His Majesty, to 1354 make good Excesses of Navy Expenditure beyond the Grants for the year ended 31st March, 1930."
Resolutions to be reported To-morrow; Committee to sit again To-morrow.

p.i: The remaining Orders were read, and postponed.

section.p: It being after half-past Eleven of the Clock upon Wednesday evening, Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER adjourned the House, without Question put, pursuant to the Standing Order.
Adjourned at Seven Minutes before One o'Clock.

housecommons.title: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
housecommons.p: The House met at a quarter before Three of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

section.title: PRIVATE BUSINESS.
section.p: City of London (Various Powers) Bill, Read the Third time, and passed.

section.title: WORK SCHEMES (LOFTUS).
section.p: 1. Mr. MANSFIELD asked the Minister of Labour what action she proposes to take in the matter of the application received by the Unemployment Grants Committee from the Loftus Urban District Council for a grant to enable them to build a retaining wall at Skinningrove for the purpose of providing work for the unemployed persons residing in that area?

p.membercontribution: : A grant from Exchequer funds in aid of this scheme was indicated to Loftus Urban District Council by letter dated 11th March.

section.title: GERMANY AND FRANCE.
section.p: 2. Mr. DAY asked the Minister of Labour whether she will give the latest information she has relating to the total number of persons recorded as unemployed in Germany and France?

p.membercontribution: : The total number of persons recorded as unemployed in Germany at 15th February, 1931, was approximately 4,991,000. In France, it has been estimated officially that, at the beginning of January, 1931, there were about 350,000 persons totally and 1,000,000 partially unemployed.
: Can my right hon. Friend say whether the German figures are issued every month?
: Yes.
: Has the right hon. Lady any information with regard to the unemployment benefit rate in Germany also?
: Yes.
: Did my right hon. Friend say that the partially unemployed in France numbered 100,000 or 1,000,000?
: One million.

section.p: 18. Sir A. POWNALL (for Sir ARTHUR STEEL-MAITLAND) asked the Minister of Labour what was the number of unemployed in Germany on the latest date available, and the estimated number of agricultural workers included in that figure?

p.membercontribution: : At the end of January, 1931, the latest date for which unemployment statistics analysed by industries are available, the total number of persons recorded as unemployed in Germany was 4,887,000, and of this number 238,359 belonged to agriculture, horticulture, cattle-breeding, forestry and fishery. Separate figures for agriculture alone are not published.

section.p: 20. Sir A. POWNALL (for Sir A. STEEL-MAITLAND) asked the Minister of Labour what is the number of women engaged in insured industry in Germany other than agriculture; and to what extent this number is in excess of what it would be if the proportion between male and female workers were the same as in insured industries in Great Britain?

p.membercontribution: : Statistics of the number of women engaged in insured industry in Germany are not in my possession.

section.title: NORFOLK FISHERMEN.
section.p: 5. Viscount ELMLEY asked the Minister of Labour if she is aware that many Norfolk fishermen pay their unemployment insurance contributions with no chance of deriving any benefit therefrom; and if she will take special steps to make it known in this area that these men may claim exemption from paying these contributions?

p.membercontribution:
: My information is that the men concerned are, in general,
1357 aware of their right to claim exemption, but if the Noble Lord has evidence to the contrary I shall be glad to consider it.
: Will the right hon. Lady be good enough to send special instructions to the Employment Exchanges in those areas, so that these misunderstandings can be avoided?
: We have done so.

section.title: TRANSFER OF WORKERS.
section.p: 13. Mr. TINKER asked the Minister of Labour how many unemployed miners have been transferred from the area covered by the Leigh Employment Exchange and the Atherton Employment Exchange during 1930 to other areas for employment in mines; and can she state how many have returned through the conditions of employment not being satisfactory?

p.membercontribution: : I am inquiring whether this information can be readily obtained; I will communicate the result to my hon. Friend as soon as possible.
: What is the position of the men who are sent to other areas where the work is unsatisfactory or is finished; do they get their railway fares back again?
: It depends upon the circumstances of the case.

section.title: BENEFIT.
section.p: 16. Mr. THOMAS LEWIS asked the Minister of Labour if she is aware that a girl of 18 years of age, without any experience away from home, has been refused unemployment benefit because she was unwilling to accept employment at sea; and whether she will take steps to ensure that benefit is not refused on such grounds?

p.membercontribution: : As my hon. Friend probably knows, the decision whether benefit should be refused rests with the statutory authorities, but if he will give me particulars of the case he has in mind, I will make inquiries.

section.title: EX-SERVICE MEN.
section.p: 17. Mr. MATTERS asked the Minister of Labour whether, seeing that many unemployed men were not of Army age when the War ended and consequently are not able to fulfil the ex-service 1358 qualification when applying for work under the schemes sanctioned by the Unemployment Grants Committee, she will take steps to reduce the ex-service men quota under such schemes from 75 per cent to 50 per cent. in those cases where the local authority requests such reduction and she is satisfied that the higher quota cannot be filled?

p.membercontribution: : The Unemployment Grants Committee have power to reduce this percentage in approved cases.

section.title: SCOTLAND.
section.p: 21. Major COLVILLE asked the Minister of Labour what is the increased number of unemployed persons in Scotland since June, 1929?

p.membercontribution: :. At 2nd March, 1931, the numbers on the registers of Employment Exchanges in Scotland showed an increase of 204,352 over the number at 3rd June, 1929.

section.title: CENSUS (APPOINTMENTS, BELPER).
section.p: 67. Mr. LEES asked the Minister of Health how many of the enumerators who have been appointed for the forthcoming taking of the Census in the town of Belper have been drawn from the unemployed signing on at the Belper Employment Exchange?

p.member: The MINISTER of HEALTH (Mr. Arthur Greenwood)
p.membercontribution: : I understand that my hon. Friend has written to the Parliamentary Secretary about this ease and that she sent to him, last night, a full statement of the facts.
: May I ask the right hon. Gentleman to reply to my question, as to how many individuals have been taken from the Employment Exchange for this work?
: I am not sure whether the hon. Member means at Belper or generally; and in either case I am afraid that I could not tell him.
: May I draw his attention to the fact that I have asked the question as to how many have been drawn from the unemployed signing on at the Employment Exchange?

: I understand that the Belper Registrar appointed the men before the circular was sent to him from
1359 the Ministry of Health. I believe two unemployed have been appointed, though not from the Employment Exchange.

: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the circular, which I understand is an appeal to Registrar to try and get men from the Employment Exchange, has never been acted upon in the town of Belper? May I ask for a reply on this point, bearing in mind the fact that the officials appointed are full-time salaried officials?
: I have already told the hon. Member that these appointments were made before the circular was issued.

section.title:
VOLUNTARY EMPLOYMENT AGENCIES
(ASSISTANCE).
section.p: 6. Mr. BATEY asked the Minister of Labour if it is her intention to continue the practice of supplying to voluntary employment agencies help from officers of the Ministry as has been supplied by her Department to the voluntary agency at Holywell Hall, Durham?

p.membercontribution: : It is not the practice to detach officers of the Ministry for work in voluntary employment agencies. I explained in an answer to the hon. Member for Barnard Castle (Mr. Lawther) on 26th February the exceptional reasons for the strictly temporary help which was given in the particular case referred to.

section.p: 7. Mr. BATEY asked the Minister of Labour the number of women clerks who were registered as unemployed at Labour Exchanges in Northumberland, Durham, and the North Riding of Yorkshire during November and December, 1930, and January and February, 1931; and whether any of those were offered the position of clerk at Holywell Hall, Durham, or as assistant at the unemployment registry in operation at Holywell Hall?

p.membercontribution: : The temporary vacancy to which I presume my hon. Friend refers was filled by the loan of a clerk employed at an Exchange who had been doing the same work previously, and the vacancy was therefore not offered to an unemployed clerk; but the arrangement resulted in the engagement temporarily of an additional clerk at the 1360 Exchange. There were no doubt a number of women clerks on the registers of the Exchanges in the area mentioned, but I could not give the exact figures without detailed inquiry.

section.title:
ROAD SCHEMES, NOTTINGHAMSHIRE
(FARM LABOURERS).
section.p: 8. Mr. SHEPHERD asked the Minister of Labour whether she is aware that the Notts county surveyor has given an assurance to the South Notts farmers' union that he will discharge farm labourers now working on road schemes; and whether she has been consulted with regard to this policy?

p.membercontribution: : I have seen a report in the Press, but have no other information on the matter, which is not one within my jurisdiction.

section.title: POTTERY AND EARTHENWARE TRADE.
section.p: 19. Sir A. POWNALL (for Sir A. STEEL-MAITLAND) asked the Minister of Labour the number of unemployed persons in the pottery and earthenware trade in January of the present year and the corresponding figures for 1929 and 1930?

p.membercontribution: : At 26th January, 1931, there were 28,040 insured persons in the pottery industry classification recorded as unemployed in Great Britain as compared with 15,097 at 27th January, 1930, and 13,485 at 21st January, 1929.

section.title: RUSSIANS (EMPLOYMENT).
section.p: 3. Mr. SMITHERS asked the Minister of Labour the nature of the employment of the 247 Russians who were admitted to this country during 1930 with Ministry of Labour permits; and how many of this number are still resident here?

p.membercontribution:
: The 247 Russians admitted to this country under Ministry of Labour permits, including four whose employment, after arrival, was agreed to by the Ministry, may be divided for employment purposes as follows: 80 concert artists, 139 theatre, cabaret and music hall artists, 4 film artists, 4 clerical workers, 3 teachers, 9 domestics and 8 miscellaneous. I am afraid I cannot give exact figures in answer to the second
1361 part of the question, but the number still resident forms a very small proportion of the total. I should add that the number covered by these permits includes natives of Russia who are not nationals of the Union of Socialist Soviet Republics but hold League of Nations certificates.
: In view of the unemployment in the theatrical profession at this time, is it advisable to continue to allow aliens to come into this country and take work away from our people?
: We have a very good arrangement now with regard to that matter.

section.title: MISS GUTHRUM BENDIKTSEN.
section.p: 27. Earl WINTERTON asked the Secretary of State for the Home Department for what reason Miss Guthrum Bendiktsen, a Danish subject, has not been granted an extension of the period for which she may remain in this country, in view of the fact that she is here for the purpose of learning English at Home-field School, Worthing, and that she has not yet attained that object?

p.member: The SECRETARY of STATE for the HOME DEPARTMENT (Mr. Clynes)
p.membercontribution: : Miss Bendiktsen was given leave to land for 12 months on the 19th January, 1930, for employment au pair at this school. When application was made to me for an extension of this period I consulted my right hon. Friend the Minister of Labour, but she was unable to recommend that an extension should be granted and I accordingly felt unable to accede to the application.

section.title: COST-OF-LIVING INDEX FIGURE.
section.p: 12. Mr. D. G. SOMERVILLE asked the Minister of Labour which of the articles used in compiling the cost-of-living index are down to pre-War level?

p.membercontribution: : The only article included in the compilation of the cost-of-living index number of which retail prices are, on average, at pre-War level is margarine.

section.title: HOURS OF LABOUR.
section.p: 14. Mr. MANDER asked the Minister of Labour to what extent standard hours of labour have been lengthened or shortened in this country and in the prin- 1362 cipal foreign countries during the last five years?

p.membercontribution: : In this country, the only industry in which, during the last five years, there has been any general change in hours of labour is coalmining. I cannot state the extent to which hours of labour have been lengthened or shortened in foreign countries.
: Is it not very important to ratify the Washington Eight Hours Convention in order to prevent the hours being lengthened?
: Certainly.

section.title:
TRADE UNIONISM (FOREIGN
COUNTRIES).
section.p: 15. Mr. MANDER asked the Minister of Labour if she has information showing in what foreign countries and to what extent the principle of compulsory trade unionism has been adopted?

p.membercontribution: : So far as I am aware, the principle of compulsory trade unionism has not been adopted in any foreign country.

section.title:
DEFAULTING RATEPAYERS
(IMPRISONMENT).
section.p: 24. Sir KINGSLEY WOOD asked the Home Secretary whether he can state generally the circumstances under which committals to prison for non-payment of rates are at present made; and whether he intends to make any proposals to the House in relation thereto?

p.membercontribution: : Where is he?
: At St. George's.
: Supporting the Conservative candidate.
: Who answers for him?
: I apologise for being late. I am afraid that I am not in a position to make any general statement and as at present advised I do not contemplate making any proposals to the House.

: Can the right hon. Gentleman indicate, at any rate, some of the information which he may have at
1363 his disposal in view of the statements recently made by two high judicial authorities?

: The Ministry of Health has rather more to do with this matter than the Home Office, and the circumstances vary so much in these cases that it is a very difficult matter to deal with them in reply to a question.

section.title: MOTORING OFFENCES (POLICE WARNINGS).
section.p: 25. Mr. DAY asked the Home Secretary the number of first warnings that have been given to motorists during the previous 12 months in the Metropolitan Police Area as an alternative to prosecution for minor motor offences?

p.membercontribution: : The total number of warnings given for minor motoring offences for the period of 12 months ended 28th February, 1931, was 35,300.
: Can my right hon. Friend say whether this is a successful method?
: I am sure that motorists prefer to be warned in the first instance rather than to have other proceedings taken.
: Is proper use made of the warning?
: Do not these extraordinary figures show how very lenient and considerate are the Police?
: I think they do.

section.title: MURDER TRIALS (DEFENCE).
section.p: 26. Mr. T. LEWIS asked the Home Secretary if he will take steps to ensure that a person against whom a capital charge has been preferred shall not be prejudiced in his defence by lack of means but that in such a case a person may claim for his defence the services of counsel of the same standing as counsel engaged by the Crown to conduct the prosecution?

p.membercontribution: : It is open to the prisoner to apply for legal aid in which event the conduct of his defence will be a matter of arrangement between him- 1364 self, his solicitor and counsel. In the event of two counsels being authorised, there is no legal obstacle to one of His Majesty's Counsel, who is willing to appear, being instructed.

section.title: WORKMEN'S COMPENSATION.
section.p: 28. Mr. TINKER asked the Home Secretary how many cases of lump-sum agreements under the Workmen's Compensation Act during 1929 were objected to by the registrar when first presented to him because the amount offered was too low; and will he say in how many cases the original sum was increased before the registrar would record the memorandum?

p.membercontribution: : As shown on page 15 of the Workmen's Compensation Statistics for 1929, the figures asked for are 1,038 and 834, respectively.
: Can my right hon. Friend tell us whether the offers were made first of all by the insurance companies or by the men's employers?
: I should require notice in order to answer that question.

section.title:
ROYAL MAIL STEAM PACKET
COMPANY.
section.p: 29. Mr. EDE asked the Home Secretary the date upon which the charter of the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company came up for revision, and the date upon which the last supplemental royal charter was granted to that company; and whether any application has been made by the company for any revision of the original charter or for the granting of a supplemental charter?

p.membercontribution: : I am informed by my Noble Friend the Lord President of the Council that supplemental charters were granted to the Royal Mail Steam Packet Company in 1851, 1852, 1904, 1912 and 1920, each of which involved a revision of the terms of the original charter conferred on the company in 1839. No application for a revision of the original charter or for the grant of a further supplemental charter is at present under consideration.

: If, and when, such an application is received, will my right hon.
1365 Friend bear in mind securing safeguards to prevent certain recent happenings in connection with this company being repeated?
: Yes, I will certainly keep that in mind.

section.title: PERFORMING BEARS.
section.p: 30. Mr. FREEMAN asked the Home Secretary whether his attention has been called to many recent accidents caused by captive bears; and whether he will consider the desirability of prohibiting the importation of performing bears into this country?

p.membercontribution: : I am not aware that there have been many accidents of this kind. I have seen a Press report of a recent case, and my attention was called to a similar incident some months ago, but I have not heard of any others. There is no power to take any action of the nature suggested.
: Is it not a fact that there was a fatal accident only last year, and that there was a very serious accident at Cardiff on Saturday?
: As I have said, all the knowledge I have on the matter is stated in my reply.
: Have any of these accidents happened in Dumbarton?

section.title: ORGANISATION AND DISTRIBUTION.
section.p: 38. Mr. HALL-CAINE asked the Home Secretary if, in view of the fact that the police are to a large extent occupied with minor offences against the Motor Car Acts and breaches of local by-laws, he will consider setting up a committee to inquire into the distribution of police duties so as to ensure a greater amount of attention to the detection and prosecution of serious crime?

p.membercontribution: : It is true that the police are called upon to perform many duties in addition to their primary duty of the maintenance of order, and the prevention and detection of crime, but these duties are nevertheless of great public value. The proper adjustment of the organisation and distribution of the 1366 police to the various duties which devolve upon theta is under the constant consideration of the police authorities and chief officers of police of the several forces, who have the advice and assistance of His Majesty's Inspectors of Constabulary if it is required, and I do not think the appointment of a committee would be likely to serve any useful purpose at the present time.

: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware of the amazing disparity between the number of prosecutions for crime between 1928 and 1911, and does he not think that a committee should be set up on this matter?
: The last report relating to this question drew attention to organisation and distribution, but the latter part of my answer makes it clear that everything is being done to deal with it.
: Is it not a fact that a very large number of cabs on the streets of London are obsolete?
: That question does not arise?
: Has the right hon. Gentleman's attention been called to a statement made by Mr. Justice McCardie on this subject?
: My attention has not been specially drawn to that statement, but I have read it.

: Even if the right hon. Gentleman is not prepared to set up a committee, will he be good enough to consider representations made by Members of this House and by representative bodies, who might like to make suggestions on this subject.
: I shall be glad to receive suggestions from any hon. Members.
: I beg to give notice that I shall raise this matter on the Adjournment of the House on an early opportunity.

section.title: THEFT (SENTENCE).
section.p:
39. Mr. FREEMAN asked the Home Secretary whether his attention has been called to the recent conviction of two men for stealing a twopenny loaf of bread
1367 who were given 28 and 14 days hard labour, respectively; and whether he will review the case with a view to reducing the sentence?

p.membercontribution: : I have made inquiry, and having regard to all the facts and circumstances of this case, and in view of the records of the two men in question, I regret I would not feel justified in advising interference with the sentences passed.

: Can the right hon. Gentleman say whether these two persons have been punished for any previous crime of which they have been guilty, whether they have been unemployed, whether they have been in receipt of unemployment benefit, and whether they pleaded in both cases that they had been starving?

section.title: NON-PROVIDED SCHOOLS.
section.p: 40. Mr. EVERARD asked the President of the Board of Education whether negotiations are still proceeding with a view to the settlement of the question of special grants to non-provided schools; and whether he has any statement to make on this matter?

p.member: The PRESIDENT of the BOARD of EDUCATION (Mr. Lees-Smith)
p.membercontribution: : I am not yet in a position to make any statement on the matter.

section.title: NURSERY SCHOOLS.
section.p: 41. Mr. MORLEY asked the President of the Board of Education what action he proposes to take to make the establishment of an adequate number of nursery schools compulsory on all local education authorities?

p.membercontribution: : I have no statutory powers to make the establishment of nursery schools compulsory.

section.title: SIZE OF CLASSES.
section.p: 42. Mr. MORLEY asked the President of the Board of Education what action he proposes to take in the near future to secure that no class in a school recognised for grant-earning purposes by the Board of Education shall exceed the number of 40 scholars on a roll?

p.membercontribution: : The policy initiated by my predecessor in 1924, and consistently pursued since, has for its immediate objective the reduction to a maximum of 40 of all classes for senior pupils, and to a maximum of 50 of those for juniors and infants. Progress, which depends mainly on the provision of new buildings, has already been substantial, and more rapid progress may be expected as the result of the great acceleration of building which has occurred in the last 18 months.

: Can the right hon. Gentleman say what steps other than making reductions in the size of classes he proposes to take in order to find employment for those additional students who were induced to enter training colleges in the last few years on the understanding that places would be found for them?

: The reduction in the size of classes depends very largely upon the provision of building accommodation, and it is the programme of building accommodation which is being pressed forward upon which I am relying.
: Can the right hon. Gentleman say whether the objective will be reached more or less concurrently by the time we get a reduction in the number of scholars owing to the declining birth-rate?
: I do not think there is any synchronisation like that.

section.title: DEFECTIVE SCHOOLS.
section.p: 43. Mr. FOOT asked the President of the Board of Education if he will furnish information, by a White Paper or otherwise, showing the several provided and non-provided schools the premises of which have been condemned by the Board and placed in division A of the black list as being unsuitable for continued recognition and incapable of improvement; and if he will show in such return the date when each school was blacklisted?

p.membercontribution: : As every local authority has been furnished with a list of the schools in its own area, I do not think there is sufficient reason for publishing a complete list. I am, however, sending a copy to the hon. Member, and if there is any further statistical information on this subject, which the hon. Member desires, I will endeavour to supply it.

section.title: NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE.
section.p: 44. Sir K. WOOD asked the Minister of Health whether he proposes to make any statement concerning the recent conclusions of the committee which has inquired into national health and other insurance schemes?

p.membercontribution: : I am not in a position to make any statement on the subject.
: Does the right hon. Gentleman propose at some early date to make a statement on this matter?
: The right hon. Gentleman knows as well as I do that it is not customary to disclose confidential reports.

: Is not this a special case? Did not the right hon. Gentleman state in regard to the prolongation of the Insurance Act that this particular committee was considering it and that they would probably make an announcement themselves?

section.p: 49. Sir K. WOOD asked the Minister of Health if he has taken any steps recently by regulations or otherwise, to afford further protection to the National Health Insurance Funds against abuse; and if he proposes to take any further action in the matter?

p.membercontribution: : Yes, Sir. Two important changes in the Medical Benefit Regulations have already been made, the first with reference to the transfer of insured persons from one doctor to another, and the second with reference to lax certification. I am also proposing, at an early date, to issue to all insurance doctors a Memorandum, and to all approved societies a circular, giving the results of the recent investigations into the increase of sickness and disablement benefit claims and advice on medical certification and the supervision of claims, respectively.

section.title: MALTA (ROYAL COMMISSION).
section.p: 45. Mr. FOOT asked the Prime Minister if he is now able to make any statement as to the composition of the Royal Commission on Malta, and as to the date when the commissioners will commence their inquiries?

p.membercontribution: : Some delay has been caused as certain of the gentlemen who have been approached with invitations to serve have been unable to relinquish their engagements in this country. An announcement will, however, be made in due course.
: Can the right hon. Gentleman say what the terms of reference will be?
: Have not they been announced?
: My impression is that they have been announced in this House.

section.title:
IMPERIAL CONFERENCE, OTTAWA
(TARIFF TRUCE).
section.p: 47. Major COLVILLE asked the Prime Minister whether, in order to place the representatives of the British Government at the Imperial Conference at Ottawa in a position to negotiate for an imperial economic policy, he will now give notice to denounce the tariff truce?

p.membercontribution: : The Commercial Convention, or tariff truce, is not yet in force, and the question of its denunciation does not, therefore, arise.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware of the feeling that exists in the Dominions that His Majesty's Government are contemplating tying their hands in this way?
: No. As a matter of fact, I know that that feeling does not exist on the part of anybody who knows the facts.
: Is it not the case that such action would effectually prevent us from taking any reciprocal action in line with—[Interruption.]

section.title: INQUIRY.
section.p:
48. Lieut.-Colonel HENEAGE asked the Prime Minister whether, as it is now a year since the announcement was made that a fishery inquiry was to be set up, he will request the committee to issue
1371 an interim report, in order that the industry may consider the information now available and act upon it, if advisable, pending the issue of a final report?

p.membercontribution: : The committee have already submitted one interim report, and I see no advantage in asking them to submit another, in view of the fact that they are now engaged in the preparation of their final report.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the interim report has already been acted upon?
: Yes.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that a report that we are going to have more coal will be more useful than this report?

section.title: EXPORT TRADE (TRAIN FERRY).
section.p: 75. Lieut.-Colonel Sir A. LAMBERT WARD asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he is pursuing a policy of arranging for the export of East Coast fish by the train ferry to Swiss and North Italian markets?

p.membercontribution: : I understand that a certain quantity of cured fish is already sent to Italy via the train ferry from Harwich. If any extension of this trade is contemplated by fish merchants I have no doubt that the railway company will provide the necessary facilities.

section.title: SHELL-FISHERIES.
section.p: 77. Lieut.-Colonel RUGGLES-BRISE asked the Minister of Agriculture what extensions have been made in British shell-fisheries during the past 12 months?

p.membercontribution: : There was no appreciable increase in the landings of shell-fish in England and Wales during 1930.

section.title: FRUIT PRESERVATION.
section.p: 50. Lieut.-Colonel RUGGLES-BRISE asked the Minister of Health if, under the regulations governing the use of 1372 chemicals employed in the preservation of imported preserved fruit and fruit pulp in this country, any of the chemicals so used are injurious to health?

p.membercontribution: : I would refer the hon. and gallant Member to the report made in 1924 by the Departmental Committee on Preservatives in Food. The general effect is that nearly all chemical preservatives are injurious or objectionable in some degree, that sulphur dioxide and its compounds—which are the preservatives used in fruit and fruit pulp—are amongst the least objectionable, and that it is necessary on practical grounds to tolerate the use of these preservatives to a limited extent. The regulations which apply equally to imported and home produced fruit are substantially in accordance with the recommendations of the committee.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman make it obligatory that there shall be a description on every jar of jam saying exactly what ingredients have been used in the production of it?
: May we take it from the right hon. Gentleman that he is of the opinion that sulphur peroxide is injurious, but that he is allowing it?
: I think the consumption of bad fruit might be even more injurious.

section.title: MILK SUPPLIES (TUBERCULOSIS).
section.p: 52. Mr. LONGBOTTOM asked the Minister of Health if he has considered a resolution of the Halifax County Borough Council requesting that, owing to the high incidence of tuberculosis among dairy cattle, he will amend the Milk and Dairies Acts of 1915 and 1926 so as to confer on local authorities the power to make compulsory the notification of all cattle arriving in their respective areas within 48 hours of arrival; and will he arrange to introduce legislation to meet this request?

p.membercontribution: : I have received this resolution from the councils of several county boroughs, and will consider it in consultation with my right hon. Friend the Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries.

section.title: CANCER (RADIOLOGICAL TREATMENT).
section.p: 57. Countess of IVEAGH asked the Minister of Health whether his Department has more recent information than that contained in the report of Public Health of 1927 with regard to the mortality following on Wertheim's operation for the treatment of cancer of the cervix uteri; and whether he will publish the known facts respecting the comparative risk from radiological treatment and the results shown in cases which have been kept under continuous observation for some years?

p.membercontribution: : The answer to the first part of the question is in the negative. The determination of the results of radiological treatment of uterine cancer, and their comparison with the results of surgical operations, are receiving continued attention, not only from the Departmental Committee on Cancer, but also from the health organisation of the League of Nations, which has arranged for the collection of international data on the subject. I am, however, advised that, in the nature of the case, it is not yet possible to make or publish effective comparisons of the risks or results as indicated in the question.
: Can the Minister of Health indicate whether he has any comparative statistics based upon the experience in this country as to these methods of treatment?
: That is one of the difficulties. I am afraid that the radiological treatment has not been sufficiently long in use to enable us to make any definite conclusions.

section.title: REFUSE DISPOSAL.
section.p: 60. Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY asked the Minister of Health whether he can make any further statement about the prevention of the dumping of town refuse by certain municipalities, or contractors acting for them, in the open country, especially in certain districts around London; and how many local authorities now dispose of refuse by incinerating?

p.membercontribution: : I have pressed the metropolitan authorities to discontinue insanitary dumps, and action has been taken or is contemplated by a number of them. Some authorities in the 1374 neighbourhood of London have made bylaws under which precautions can be enforced to prevent any nuisance from refuse tips. Returns for the year 1928–29 from 216 of the larger urban authorities show that 138–19 being in London—incinerated part or the whole of their refuse.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman taking any steps to deal with what cannot be dealt with under any by-law—the colossal dumps that are left?
: That is one of the matters which are now under discussion.
: Have the Government any powers to prevent damping of other kinds?
: Is this matter being dealt with, as was promised by the Parliamentary Secretary, in the proposed Town Planning Bill?
: The hon. and gallant Member must wait for the Bill.

section.title: BIRTH CERTIFICATES.
section.p: 63. Mr. ALBERY asked the Minister of Health if he bas had brought to his notice the traffic in bogus British birth certificates; and whether he is now prepared to consider with the Home Office precautions for the prevention of the misuse of birth certificates?

p.membercontribution: : Nothing further on the subject has come to my notice since the hon. Member's previous question in November last, when, as I may remind him, I informed him that I was not clear as to the nature of the precautions which he had in mind but that I would consider any cases of which particulars were given to me.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware of the statements made in the Press that the Home Office is inquiring into the fraudulent use of these birth certificates abroad?
: That question should be addressed to the Home Secretary.
: But will the right hon. Gentleman consult with the Home Office on this matter?
: I have already done so.

section.title: MATERNAL MORTALITY.
section.p: 64. Mr. LEACH asked the Minister of Health what is the method used by his Department to calculate maternal mortality rates; and how long after the birth is the death of the mother included in the tables?

p.membercontribution: : The selection of the deaths for inclusion in the maternal mortality rates published by the Registrar-General is governed by the medical certificate that death was directly or indirectly due to certain causes, and does not depend upon the time which elapsed between the confinement and the death.

section.title: VACCINATION.
section.p: 66. Mr. LEACH asked the Minister of Health whether, in view of the recommendation given on page 72 of the last report of the Rolleston Committee on Vaccination in regard to the use of anti-vaccinal serum to mitigate the dangerous encephalitic effects of vaccination, which shows that, notwithstanding the improved methods of performing the operation which have recently been introduced, it is still impossible to guarantee that it will not be followed by nervous complications of a serious character, he will either cease to enforce the operation or compensate the parents in cases where dangerous results arise?

p.membercontribution: : I have no power to suspend or vary the provisions of the Vaccination Acts, which do not provide for the payment of compensation in such cases as my hon. Friend mentions. I may however point out that the compulsory requirements of the Acts are in effect limited to infants under 12 months of age, and that in this class the occurrence of post-vaccinal encephalitis has been practically negligible.
: Has anything been done to provide still newer serum in order to counteract the ill-effects of the anti-vaccinal serum?
: I must ask for notice of that question.

section.title: NON-PARLOUR HOUSES (COST).
section.p: 51. Mr. WELLOCK asked the Minister of Health the average superficial area and the average price of A-type non-parlour 1376 houses in direct labour schemes and in contracts let by local authorities in England and Wales during 1930?

p.membercontribution: : The average superficial area was 761 feet, and the average price, £340.

section.title: TOWN PLANNING (RIBBON DEVELOPMENT).
section.p: 55. Mr. EDE asked the Minister of Health if the promised legislation on town planning will include any proposals to restrict ribbon development?

p.membercontribution: : Pending the introduction of the Bill, I fear that I cannot say more than that this aspect of planning is receiving my careful consideration.
: Can the right hon. Gentleman say when he intends to introduce the Bill?
: I hope that it will be at an early date.
: Has it been approved by the Liberal party?

section.title: OXTED AND LIMPSFIELD.
section.p: 56. Mr. EDE asked the Minister of Health what is the present position of the Godstone Rural District Council with regard to the provision of additional houses in the parishes of Oxted and Limpsfield?

p.membercontribution: : I have been informed by the district council that they propose to provide 24 additional houses in these parishes.

section.title:
CONDITIONS OF TENANCY (LIGHTING AND
HEATING).
section.p: 59. Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY asked the Minister of Health whether he is aware that cases have occurred recently of local authorities forbidding tenants on housing estates a free choice of gas or electricity for lighting, cooking purposes, etc.; and what attitude he is adopting In such cases?

p.membercontribution: : I would refer my hon. and gallant Friend to the reply given on the 26th ultimo to a question on the subject by my hon. Friend, the Member for Plaistow (Mr. W. Thorne) of which I am sending him a copy.
: Has the right hon. Gentleman been able to take any further action in this matter?
: No, I have taken the line of leaving it to local authorities.
: Have local authorities been informed that is is undesirable to differentiate between one industry and another?
: I cannot generalise on that, as circumstances vary in different areas.
: Is this a practical example of Socialist principles at work?

section.title: SLUM CLEARANCES (KENT).
section.p: 61. Mr. ALBERY asked the Minister of Health what progress has been made in slum clearance in Kent during the last 12 months?

p.membercontribution: : During the past 12 months arrangements have been made for the acquisition of all the properties comprised in the only slum clearance scheme made under the old legislation in the county of Kent. As regards progress under the Housing Act, 1930, I am sending the hon. Member a copy of the reply given by me to a question put by my hon. Friend, the Member for Dartford (Mr. Mills) on the 21st January last. Since the date of that reply one area in the county, occupied by 420 persons, has been declared a clearance area.
: Is the right hon. Gentleman taking any steps to expedite the present slum clearance schemes?
: Yes, now that the county council elections are over.

section.title: LAND DRAINAGE ACT, 1930.
section.p: 62. Mr. ALBERY asked the Minister of Health in what cases he has exercised the powers conferred upon him by the Land Drainage Act of 1930?

p.membercontribution: : I presume the hon. Member refers to the power conferred on me by the Act of making Provisional Orders of my own motion for constituting Joint Committees for the prevention of pollution. This power has not yet been exercised. I would refer at the same time to my reply of 5th instant to a question by the hon. Member for Lancaster (Mr. Ramsbotham).
: Can the right hon. Gentleman say whether he intends to exercise these powers?
: Yes. If the hon. Member will read my reply to an earlier question he will see what is contemplated.

section.title: POOR LAW (TEST WORK).
section.p: 65. Mr. LONGDEN asked the Minister of Health the names of the public assistance authorities under which outdoor relief is given to able-bodied men without any conditions as to test work; and if he can say whether it is under his order that the Birmingham public assistance committee is about to cause all able-bodied men applying for relief for a longer period than four weeks to do compulsory work for a minimum of four days a week at eight hours a day, with one hour for dinner, irrespective of the amount of relief paid to the applicants?

p.membercontribution: : Test work may have various meanings, but on the widest interpretation there are 32 public assistance authorities who are requiring no form of work as a condition of the grant of relief to able-bodied men. I am sending my hon. Friend a list. In the areas of 15 of these authorities the numbers of able-bodied men are so small or so scattered that a scheme is at present impracticable. In the remaining 17 areas schemes of work or training are in various stages of consideration. As regards the second part of the question, I have urged upon the Birmingham public assistance authority, in the interests of the men, that the hours of work should be uniform and that the period of six weeks during which they had been granted unconditional relief should be reduced to four weeks. I have not in fact suggested the number of hours, but I should not regard 32 hours a week as more than adequate to secure the object of improving or maintaining the man's employability.
: Is the Minister of Health satisfied that the suggested 28 hours per week as a minimum of work for a single applicant for relief is enough in face of the maximum of about 15s. per week in relief?
: In connection with training schemes the amount of training settles the number of hours, irrespective of the relief.
: Has the right hon. Gentleman done away with stone-breaking, which he has said was so brutal? [HON. MEMBERS: "Yes !"] No, he has not.

section.title: BUDGET.
section.p: 68. Mr. GRAHAM WHITE asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer if he is prepared to give consideration to the proposal that the taxation of motor cars over a certain age should be reduced?

69. Mr. D. G. SOMERVILLE asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether he will consider introducing into the Finance Bill proposals to relieve the clergy from the payment of Income Tax on voluntary Whitsuntide offerings of their congregations?

p.member: The FINANCIAL SECRETARY to the TREASURY (Mr. Pethick-Lawrence)
p.membercontribution: : My right hon. Friend is not prepared to anticipate his Budget statement.
: Will the hon. Gentleman bear in mind that such a change might well have a favourable influence on the revenue, as old motors consume more petrol?
: The hon. Gentleman may rest assured that that point and all other relevant matters will be taken into consideration.

section.title:
GERMAN REPARATIONS AND INTER-ALLIED
DEBTS.
section.p: 70. Lieut.-Colonel Sir FREDERICK HALL asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer what amount this country is due to receive this year from the German reparations payment and from the Dominions in respect of war debts; and what will be the amount due to be paid in the same year to the United States under the war debts settlement with America?

p.membercontribution: : The amount to be received during the financial year from the current German reparation annuities is £16,300,000, and from allied debts £17,700,000, making a 1380 total of £34,000,000 as against the £33,000,000 due to be paid during the same period to the United States Government in respect of the British war debt. The receipts from the Dominions during the same period amount to £7,632,300, but these receipts represent the reimbursement to the United Kingdom of the cost of the moneys borrowed in this country on behalf of the Dominions, and cannot be reckoned as a set-off against our American debt payment.

section.title: INCOME TAX (COLLECTION).
section.p: 71. Sir F. HALL asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer whether the Government have yet reached a decision regarding the proposed transfer of the control of the collectors of Income Tax from the local commissioners to the Board of Inland Revenue?

p.membercontribution: : My right hon. Friend is not in a position at the present time to anticipate his Budget statement in this or any other respect.

: Is it not a fact that we are not asking for an anticipation of the Budget statement; and will the hon. Gentleman say "Yes" or "No" to the question as to whether the Government have decided to make this alteration and to bring these collectors immediately under the Inland Revenue office?
: The answer to that question is that the Government have not yet come to a decision on the matter.

: Is there not a suspicion of the Government doing that? [Laughter.] Hon. Members opposite do not understand, but I am sure that the hon. Gentleman recognises the fact that this is a very important point as to whether there is going to be this liaison, between the taxpayer and the Government service.
: The fact that the hon. and gallant Gentleman has a suspicion apparently answers that question in the affirmative.

section.title: TURPENTINE AND WHITE SPIRIT (REVENUE).
section.p: 72. Mr. WHITE asked the Chancellor of the Exchequer the amount of revenue derived from the tax on turpentine and white spirit in 1929 and 1930?

p.membercontribution: : The amount of revenue derived from white spirit cannot be given, as this substance is not separately classified in the official accounts, but is included under the heading of "Petroleum spirit, other than motor spirit." The net amount of revenue derived from the duty on turpentine and petroleum spirit, other than motor spirit, during each of the calendar years 1929 and 1930, was as follows:

tr.td: Petroleum spirit, other than motor spirit.

section.title: IMPORTED FRUIT PULP.
section.p: 74. Lieut.-Colonel RUGGLES-BRISE asked the Minister of Agriculture if he will consider introducing a Bill, amending the Merchandise Marks Act, to insist upon a description of an imported article such as fruit pulp, which after reaching this country undergoes a material change on conversion into jam, being given on all containers of jam, together with the country of origin and the percentages of all the ingredients?

p.membercontribution: : After careful consideration, I have come to the conclusion that the difficulties of enforcing a Marking Order under the Merchandise Marks Act, 1926, would be so great that no advantage would be gained by amending the Act for the purpose. The most promising solution appears to be to bring jam made from home-grown fruit within the scope of the National Mark scheme, and I am considering the possibility of introducing the legislation which I am advised is necessary to enable this to be done.
: Can the right hon. Gentleman give any idea as to when that legislation is likely to be introduced?
: We would not, of course, legislate on a matter of this sort 1382 unless there was agreement, and I am doing my best to see what measure of agreement can be obtained.

section.title: SMALLHOLDING, ESSEX (PURCHASE).
section.p: 78. Mr. PYBUS asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he is aware that Mr. A. F. Carnell, an ex-service man of Clacton-on-Sea, having occupied a smallholding for seven years and secured fourth prize in all Essex in the smallholders' competition, has made application to be allowed to purchase his holding; that on the recommendation of the smallholdings and allotments subcommittee of the Essex County Council his application has not been approved by the Ministry of Agriculture; and that the Essex County Council as an alternative has now, after a lapse of six months, offered to Mr. Carnell a portion of another man's smallholding upon which they are prepared to expend public money for the erection of a house and buildings upwards of a quarter of a mile from Mr. Carnell's present holding, the rent of which on a 5 per cent. basis would be more than treble Mr. Carnell's present rent, and whereby Mr. Carnell would be sacrificing, not only the goodwill of his present business, but the results of eight years' cultivation of his existing holding; and whether, in these circumstances, the Minister will withdraw his consent to the refusal by the Essex County Council for Mr. Carnell to acquire his present holding?

p.membercontribution: : All the facts mentioned in the first part of the question were before me when, after careful consideration of all the circumstances, I decided to consent to the county council's refusal of Mr. Carnell's application. There is no intention on the part of the council to deprive him of the tenancy of his present holding, and the proposals described in the second part of the question, which have doubtless been made to meet Mr. Carnell's desire for the ownership of a holding, do not afford sufficient ground for reviewing my decision.

: Will the right hon. Gentleman say whether this ex-service man has not fulfilled all his part of the bargain; and whether he is not within his rights in asking to be allowed to purchase this holding instead of merely renting it?

: This ex-service man is, I have no doubt, a very good man, and
1383 he is quite within his rights in asking to be allowed to purchase the holding, but the county council are also within their rights in not wishing to sell it. The existence of a semi-detached house and of a footpath at this point and other reasons, seem to be quite good reasons for the county council not wishing to sell.
: On a point of Order. May I ask for the guidance of hon. Members whether a question of this length and character affecting a single individual is not an abuse of the time of this House?
: I should not like to lay down a Rule on that point.
: In view of the unsatisfactory answer given by the right hon. Gentleman, I propose to raise this matter on the Adjournment of the House at the earliest convenient opportunity.

section.title: SUGAR-BEET WORKERS, SUFFOLK (WAGES).
section.p: 79. Mr. LEES asked the Minister of Agriculture whether, in view of the fact that public subsidies are paid to the farmers in Suffolk in respect of sugar-beet, he will consider the advisability of making it a condition of the granting of such subsidies that higher rates of wages shall be paid to the employés in this industry?

p.membercontribution: : The subsidy under the British Sugar Subsidy Act, 1925, is not paid direct to beet growers but to the companies owning the factories where the sugar is manufactured. Section 3 of the British Sugar Subsidy Act, 1925, makes provision for fair wages to be paid by factory companies in receipt of subsidy by saying that the wages paid shall, except where paid at a rate agreed upon by a joint industrial council representing the employer and the persons employed, not be less than would be payable if the manufacture were carried on under a contract made between the Minister and the employer containing a fair wage clause which complied with the requirements of any resolution of the House of Commons for the time being in force, applicable to contracts of Government Departments. The wages of all farm workers are subject to the minimum rates fixed by the Agricultural Wages Committees.

: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware of the attempt to reduce the wages of the workers referred to from 30s. to 28s. a week; and is he not prepared to take steps, or can he not find time to take steps to secure a guaranteed rate of wages for these workers?
: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that in Suffolk some of the growers are unable to renew their contracts with the factories receiving the subsidy?
: I am not aware of that, but I do not think it arises out of the question.
: Will the right hon. Gentleman take steps to ensure that where the wages are reduced the subsidy also shall be reduced?

: I may say that I am doing everything I can in connection with the matter mentioned by my hon. Friend the Member for Belper (Mr. Lees). With regard to the subsidy, the growers in Suffolk are not receiving it because the Anglo-Dutch sugar factory are not making use of the offer.
: Is there not an arrangement by which the grower of beet is guaranteed a certain price from the factory?
: There is some arrangement prevailing, but it does not prevail, I am sorry to say, in Suffolk except as regards one factory.
: Are not the majority of sugar-beet workers pieceworkers?

section.title:
LEICESTERSHIRE AND RUTLAND (WAGES
AND HOURS).
section.p: 80. Mr. LEES asked the Minister of Agriculture if he is aware that the Leicestershire and Rutland agricultural wages committee propose to increase the working hours in agriculture in these two counties to 56½ hours a week for eight months of the year and to increase the working hours for the other four months in Rutland to 54 a week without any increase in wages; and will he now consider introducing a Bill to give to the Agricultural Wages Board full powers to review and revise decisions arrived at by the agricultural wages committees?

p.membercontribution: : I am aware that this committee has given notice of a proposal to vary, as stated, the hours on which the weekly minimum wage is based. As, however, I informed my hon. Friend on the 19th February, I am afraid legislation giving wider powers to the Agricultural Wages Board is impracticable at the present time.
: Can the right hon. Gentleman say why so much time is given to benefit the farmer and not the worker?
: We all recognise that, if we get the industry into a sound condition, it will be in a position to pay good wages.

section.title:
NEW GOVERNMENT BUILDINGS,
WHITEHALL (TIMBER).
section.p: 81. Mr. LESLIE BOYCE asked the First Commissioner of Works whether the Government will specify that Empire timber only is to be used in the building of the new Government offices at Whitehall?

p.member: The FIRST COMMISSIONER of WORKS (Mr. Lansbury)
p.membercontribution: : The proposals for the erection of the building to which the hon. Member refers have not yet reached the stage at which it is necessary to consider the materials to be used.

: Will the right hon. Gentleman bear in mind that there is ample variety and quantity of Empire timbers for this purpose, and that both the Dominions and Colonial Governments in similar circumstances give a preference to British materials?
: All that is taken into account.

section.title:
GOVERNMENT OFFICIALS, EAST
AFRICA (TRAVELLING EXPENSES).
section.p: 82. Mr. BOYCE asked the Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies if he is now in a position to state the amount paid by the Government during 1930 to British and foreign steamship companies, respectively, in respect of passages for Government officials carried between Great Britain and East Africa?

p.member: The UNDER-SECRETARY of STATE for the COLONIES (Dr. Drummond Shiels)
p.membercontribution: : No, Sir; but my Noble Friend has asked the Governments of the East 1386 African Dependencies to forward the necessary information, and it will be communicated to the hon. Member when received.
: Would not the hon. Gentleman find it simpler if his Department rang up the Crown Agent or the shipping companies to find out?
: No, Sir.
: May I press the hon. Gentleman—
: The hon. Member is asking on a matter of opinion.

section.title: HONG KONG (MUI-TSAI SYSTEM).
section.p: 83. Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies why the orders contained in the despatch of the Secretary of State, dated 22nd August, 1929, to the effect that steps were to be taken forthwith to set up machinery for the inspection, control and remuneration of the existing mui-tsai in Hong Kong have not been carried out by the Governor?

p.membercontribution: : The hon. Member is under a misapprehension in thinking that the Secretary of State's instructions have not been carried out. I will place in the Library a copy of the regulations made by the Governor in Council on the 7th of November, 1929, providing for the regulation and remuneration of existing mui-tsai in Hong Kong.
: Have these regulations been carried out?

: Yes, as far as we know, they have been carried out in their entirety, and a report has already been placed in the Library giving the effect of the six months' working of these regulations. If the hon. Member has any case brought to his notice which suggests otherwise, I should be glad to know.
: Is the hon. Gentleman contented with what has been done?
: Yes.

section.title:
IRAQ PETROLEUM COMPANY
(LABOUR CONDITIONS).
section.p:
84. Mr. THORNE asked the Under-Secretary of State for the Colonies whether his attention has been called to
1387 the fact that the convention regulating the transition of the mineral oil of the Iraq Petroleum Company, Limited, through the territory of Palestine contains no clause for safeguarding fair wages and labour conditions or for labour legislation under the convention; and what steps he intends to take with a view to rectifying the omission?

p.membercontribution: : Yes, Sir; my Noble Friend is aware that there is no such clause in the agreement. The point is engaging his attention.
: Will the hon. Gentleman do his level best to see that the Arabs and Jews will have a minimum rate of pay while putting down this pipe track?
: Yes, we are going into the matter now.

section.title: ARGENTINE.
section.p: 85. Mr. HANNON asked the President of the Board of Trade whether he is now in a position to state whether the Argentine Government have yet decided to introduce an emergency tariff; and if any reply has been received to the representations which he has made to the Argentine Government?

p.membercontribution: : Particulars of increases in the import duties on certain kinds of goods and of the imposition of duties upon other goods hitherto admitted free into the Argentine were published in the "Board of Trade Journal" of the 5th March. No representations in regard to these measures have yet been made to the Argentine Government, but the position is being carefully watched.
: I did not ask the hon. Member about past tariffs; I am asking if he has any information about a proposed emergency tariff in future, and what representations have been made?

: There is a great, deal of information at the disposal of the Department, but the matter is one of singular difficulty; I can assure my hon. Friend that the interests of British trade will be protected.

section.title: RUSSIA.
section.p: 86. Sir F. HALL asked the President of the Board of Trade whether he can give an approximate estimate of the number of persons who have been directly or indirectly employed as a result of the total exports to Soviet Russia of United Kingdom goods and productions during 1930, valued at £6,500,000?

p.membercontribution: : I regret that this information is not available.
: Is the Minister aware that because of the promise that the restoration of trade with Russia would considerably reduce unemployment, many Socialists were returned at the last General Election?
: Is it not a fact—[Interruption.]
: Major Colville.
: May I ask a supplementary question?
: I have called the next question.
: I was on my feet, Mr. Speaker.
: I did not hear the hon. Member.
: Is that not because there is so much noise?

section.title: TARIFFS.
section.p: 87. Major COLVILLE asked the President of the Board of Trade which foreign countries have increased their tariffs against British goods since June, 1929?

p.membercontribution: : Tariff increases which may be regarded as of some general importance to British trade by reason of their nature or their scope have come into force in the following countries since the date mentioned, namely:—Argentina, Austria, Bulgaria, Chile, China, Czechoslovakia, Egypt, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iran, Italy, Mexico. Netherlands, East Indies, Persia, Peru, Portugal, Turkey and the United States. In numerous other foreign countries there have been increases of a minor character or of restricted scope. In a number of cases the increases on some articles have been accompanied by decreases on others.
: In view of that answer, can the hon. Gentleman say whether the Government are still optimistic about securing a Tariff Truce?

section.p: Viscountess ASTOR rose—

p.membercontribution: : Answer!
: The Noble Lady had better wait until a reply has been given.
: The reply to the hon. and gallant Member is that the Government are always optimistic.
: Have any Dominions increased their tariffs?
: Notice had better be given of that question.
: Can the hon. Gentleman say how many of the countries which have increased their tariffs have signed the Tariff Truce?
: Notice should be given of that question.

section.title:
INTERNATIONAL COLONIAL EXHIBITION,
PARIS.
section.p: 89. Mr. D. G. SOMERVILLE asked the Secretary to the Overseas Trade Department what foreign Governments are participating in the main part of the forth-coming International Colonial Exhibition in Paris; and whether the decision that His Majesty's Government shall not participate in this exhibition can be reconsidered?

p.membercontribution: : My hon. Friend is informed that, in addition to the French Colonies, the Governments of Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Portugal and the United States of America are erecting pavilions. I am afraid the answer to the last part of the question must be in the negative.
: In view of the success of the recent trade exhibition in this country, would it not be advisable for the Government to take part in this exhibition so as to secure orders for this country?
: I understand that a very full answer was given to the previous question by my right hon. Friend.

section.title:
ANGLO-HUNGARIAN CLEARING
OFFICE.
section.p: 88. Sir A. LAMBERT WARD asked the President of the Board of Trade the date upon which it is proposed that the Anglo-Hungarian clearing office will make a further distribution in respect of interest upon admitted claims in the terms of the announcement in the official circular issued from Cornwall House, dated 7th November, 1930?

p.membercontribution: : It is hoped that sufficient funds will become available to enable a further distribution to be made in respect of interest in the Hungarian Administration towards the end of the year.
: Is there any intention of closing down this clearing office?
: I cannot say.

section.title: LOSS OF AIRSHIP R 101 (INQUIRY).
section.p: 90. Sir WILLIAM MITCHELL-THOMSON asked the Under-Secretary of State for Air whether the report upon R 101 has yet been received by the Ministry; and when it will be published?

91. Lieut.-Commander KENWORTHY asked the Under-Secretary of State for Air whether the report of the Committee of Inquiry into the loss of R 101 will be at the disposal of Members before the Air Estimates are discussed; and, if not, when he expects the report to be available?

p.member: The UNDER-SECRETARY of STATE for AIR (Mr. Montague)
p.membercontribution: : The report has not yet been received by the Air Ministry, but I understand that it is complete and in the hands of the printers, save for a section dealing with the experiments carried cut recently at the National Physical Laboratory. As I stated in my reply to the hon. Member for Bedford (Mr. Wells) on 25th February, these experiments are considered to be of material value, and my Noble Friend concurs with the Court of Inquiry in thinking that the report ought to include a reference to their results. On this basis my Noble Friend is informed that the Court hope that the report will be available for publication by the end of the month.

: Will the hon. Member represent to his Noble Friend that it would be extremely desirable if it is possible that this report should be available before the Air Estimates are taken on Report stage even if it cannot be available for Committee stage?
: My Noble Friend is not responsible for the date at which the report will be presented.
: Could not the part of the Air Estimates dealing with airships be postponed until we have this very important document?

: May I again ask the hon. Member if he will represent to his Noble Friend that it will be very difficult for this House to part with the Air Estimates on the Report stage without having had an opportunity of considering this matter, and that as the major portion of the report is already available it is very desirable that the whole report should be matte available for Members here.
: It will of course, be possible to discuss the report on one of the later Supply days.
: Will the Under-Secretary give an undertaking that the Report stage of the Estimates will not be taken until the report is in the hands of hon. Members provided that it is issued before 30th March.
: I cannot give such an undertaking.

section.title: SUB-POSTMASTERS (REMUNERATION).
section.p: 93. Mr. GORDON MACDONALD asked the Postmaster-General the total number of scale - payment sub - postmasters; the average rate of their remuneration; the average rate of reduction owing to the recent bonus cut; the number who will now be in receipt of emoluments not exceeding £100 per annum; and the number receiving not more than £75 per annum?

p.membercontribution: : According to the latest available figures, the total number of scale-payment sub-postmasters is approximately 21,000. The average rate of remuneration is about £115 a year 1392 and the average rate of reduction as a result of the recent alteration in bonus £6 a year. The numbers in receipt of inclusive emoluments not exceeding (a) £100 and (b) £75 are roughly 13,000 and 11,000, respectively.

(by Private Notice) asked the Secretary for Mines whether he is aware that limestone works in Derbyshire are being compelled to close owing to a shortage of coal and that large numbers of men are being thrown out of work, and what action he proposes to take in the matter?

: I notice that the Noble Lord, in putting his question, introduces some information which is not contained in the question submitted to me. He refers to the district in which this alleged shortage occurs, and that is not contained in the question. The question put to me is: "To ask the Minister of Mines whether he is aware that limestone works are being compelled to close owing to a shortage of coal, that large numbers of men are being thrown out of work, and can anything be done?"
: Limestone works in Derbyshire.

: The reply is: I have had no complaint from limestone works of any shortage of coal until the Noble Lord a few minutes ago informed me about the matter. I will have the matter looked into and will communicate with him.

: As the hon. Member has said that I did not give him notice, may I say that immediately on receiving this telegram I telephoned to the head permanent officer in his Department informing him that the limestone works were in Derbyshire? May I ask him whether he is aware that there is only one district in Derbyshire where there are limestone works; and may I have an answer to the question?
: I was not aware that there is only one limestone works in Derbyshire. I have told the Noble Lord that I will have this matter inquired into and will communicate with him.
: May I ask the Prime Minister what the business will be for next week?

: Monday: Representation of the People (No. 2) Bill, Committee; 3rd Allotted Day.
Tuesday: Motion, "That Mr. Speaker do leave the chair on going into Committee of Supply on Air Estimates." In Committee, Air Estimates, Votes A 1, 4, 3, and 8. Ways and Means Resolution in Committee.
Wednesday: Supply, 2nd Allotted Day. Report of Navy Estimate 1931, Navy Supplementary Estimate 1930, and Navy Excess 1929.
Thursday: Supply, 3rd Allotted Day. Civil Estimates and Estimates for Revenue Departments; Vote on Account; Report.
The business for Friday will be announced later.
: May I ask the Leader of the House what subjects will be taken on the Report of the Vote on Account, and who will have the right to select those subjects?
: The selection will be made by the Liberals below the Gangway. They have not yet handed in the subjects which they wish to have discussed. Perhaps they may be announced later.

: May I ask the right hon. Gentleman: Are the Liberals given these facilities because they are regarded by the Government as a section of the Opposition, or are they given them as reward for faithful services?

: The right hon. Gentleman has no business to make that suggestion. [Interruption.] The present Government can be trusted to carry on the rules and traditions of this House, whether right hon. Gentlemen opposite sneer or not. The party that has the right to choose the subjects is a part of the Opposition.

: Are not the arrangements made in precise accordance with the precedents which have been set; and is it not in accordance with the practice that has been followed in this Parliament that the Liberal party should have its turn in choosing?

: Since both the Prime Minister and the right hon. Gentleman the Member for Darwen (Sir H. Samuel) appeal to the rules and traditions of the House, may I not ask whether it is not the fact that in the 1906 Parliament, when the Liberal party were in a majority and were holding office, neither the Nationalists nor the Labour party were given such a choice of subjects?
: That was not the case.

section.title:
LONDON PASSENGER TRANSPORT
BILL,
section.p: "to provide for the establishment of a Passenger Transport Board for the London traffic area and for the transfer to that Board of the various transport undertakings and interests; to make other provisions with respect to traffic in the said area; and for purposes connected with the matters aforesaid," presented by Mr. Herbert Morrison; supported by Mr. Clynes, Mr. William Graham, the Solicitor-General, and Mr. Pethick-Lawrence; to be read a Second time upon Monday next, and to be printed. [Bill 109.]

section.title: MESSAGE FROM THE LORDS.
section.p: That they have passed a Bill, intituled, "An Act to provide for the reception and detention of certain persons of unsound mind in the Royal Naval Hospital at Great Yarmouth and for the treatment therein of certain voluntary patients; to prohibit the taking of legal proceedings in respect of the reception and detention of any person in the said hospital before the commencement of this Act; and for purposes connected with the matters aforesaid." [Yarmouth Naval Hospital Bill [Lords.]

body.p: Mr. MILLS asked the Minister of Health how many local authorities have housing plans in prospect in the counties of Lancashire and Yorkshire, and the total number of houses contemplated within the next five years?

Mr. GREENWOOD: I assume my hon. Friend refers to the programmes which the larger local authorities are required by the Act of 1930 to submit. Sixty-seven programmes have been received from Lancashire and Yorkshire, and the total number of houses contemplated in the next five years by these local authorities is 92,957.

Dr. SALTER asked the Minister of Health the average cost of non-parlour and parlour houses in contracts let by, and in approved direct labour schemes of, local authorities in England and Wales during each of the years ended 31st December, 1927, 1928, 1929, and 1930?

Mr. GREENWOOD: The following statement shows the desired particulars:
Year. Non-parlour houses. Parlour houses.
£ £
1927 … … 413 480
1928 … … 362 429
1929 … … 345 409
1930 … … 340 404

Sir K. WOOD asked the Minister of Health the average cost of non-parlour and parlour houses in contracts let by and in approved direct labour schemes of local authorities in England and Wales at the last convenient date?
Mr. GREENWOOD: For the month of January, 1931, the average figures were: for non-parlour houses £349, and for parlour houses £396.

Brigadier-General CLIFTON BROWN asked the Minister of Health whether he 1396 will arrange for a study to be made of the relative nutritional values of the different types of milk which are on sale, either by the Medical Research Council or by the committee which the Government have recently set up to study the nutrition of the nation; and whether the research experiments of the Dairy Research Institute at Shinfield in that direction will be carefully considered?
Mr. GREENWOOD: I will consider the hon. and gallant Member's suggestion.
Countess of IVEAGH asked the Minister of Health whether he will obtain from all institutions using radium the record of their follow-up results from year to year?

Mr. GREENWOOD: I understand that arrangements have been made by the Radium Commission to obtain annual returns showing these results from the radium centres to which radium is lent by the Commission. I will consider the question of obtaining similar returns from local authorities in whose institutions radium is used.

Mr. FREEMAN asked the Minister of Health how many persons were diagnosed as having died from cancer during 1930; whether he has record of how many of these persons were habitual consumers of flesh foods, beer or spirits, or non-flesh diet; and whether, if such details are not available, he will instruct all registrars of deaths to furnish them in future?

Mr. GREENWOOD: The number of deaths registered during 1930 in England and Wales and classified to cancer was 57,870. This figure is provisional. No information is available with regard to the matters referred to in the second part of the question. As regards the third part, registrars of births and deaths are not entitled to obtain any information with respect to a death other than that relating to the particulars required by law to be registered, and it would not therefore be possible to adopt my hon. Friend's suggestion.

Mr. LONGDEN asked the Minister of Health how many able-bodied persons were in receipt of outdoor relief in the county of London on 1st March last; and the number of such persons who were receiving relief without the imposition of a work or other test?

Mr. GREENWOOD: On Saturday, 28th February last, the number of able-bodied men in receipt of outdoor relief in the county of London was 4,959, and of these 3,733 were receiving such relief without the imposition of a work or other test.

Sir K. WOOD asked the Minister of Health, according to the latest available information based on the figures for the standard year, the amount per head of the estimated population in 1928 of the Exchequer grant payable annually during the first fixed grant period under the Local Government Act, 1929, to the borough council of Woolwich, and the sum by which the amount exceeds the losses on account of rates and grants attributable to the operation of the Act?

Mr. GREENWOOD: According to the latest available information based on the figures for the standard year (1928–29), the general Exchequer grant under the Local Government Act, 1929, payable annually during the first fixed grant period to the council of the Metropolitan borough of Woolwich, amounts to 7s. 5d. per head of the estimated population in 1928 of the borough. The share of the borough in the Exchequer grants payable annually during the first fixed grant period under the Act to the borough council and to the London County Council amounts to 13s. 8d. per head of the estimated population of the borough and exceeds the loss otherwise attributable to the operation of the Act, as calculated on the figures of the standard year, by £9,150 or 1s. 3d. per head of the estimated population of the borough.
